📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

It has been revealed that the significant AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for customers is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Industry observers note that accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all owners that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly states that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

Sources indicate that to set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI states users accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Recent findings suggest that gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

In a recent development, for all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health complications like eating disorders.

Recent findings suggest that these protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

As with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly rapidly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

It has been revealed that meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All owners, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Apple customers have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

In a recent development, the new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of users, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Industry observers note that like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Owners must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

Industry observers note that if you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says users identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

Industry observers note that more generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence.".

Sources indicate that there is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

It has been revealed that claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide customers towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the massive seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

Breaking: Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that 40 years ago, the crime drama “Heat” opened in France and received positive reviews from Paris critics.
  • In a recent development, american reviewers dismissed “Heat” with casual cruelty, but as so often happens in film history — think Jerry Lewis, Michael Cimino’s “Heaven’s Gate,” or Brian De Palma’s “Mission to Mars” — the French got our cinema right where our own critics got it embarrassingly wrong.
  • From early on, one of the most interesting things about Burt Reynolds was the tension between his affable onscreen persona — the smiling, charming fellow who had major box office hits with crowd-pleasers like “Smokey and the Bandit” and “The Cannonball Run” — and the visible agitation simmering underneath.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that 40 years ago, the crime drama “Heat” opened in France and received positive reviews from Paris critics. No, not the “Heat” directed by Michael Mann that starred Robert De Niro and Al Pacino and would go on to become a revered classic — that came nine years later. The “Heat” that played in Europe in 1986 starred Burt Reynolds, was directed by multiple journeyman helmers, and was almost immediately forgotten only months after it limped into U.S. theaters in March of 1987.

In a recent development, american reviewers dismissed “Heat” with casual cruelty, but as so often happens in film history — think Jerry Lewis, Michael Cimino’s “Heaven’s Gate,” or Brian De Palma’s “Mission to Mars” — the French got our cinema right where our own critics got it embarrassingly wrong. “Heat,” in which Reynolds plays an aging mercenary held prisoner by a crippling gambling addiction, is not only one of Reynolds’ most interesting films but one of his most personal, and a top-tier entry in the canon of the subgenre that is “Burt Noir.” Related Stories Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors.

From early on, one of the most interesting things about Burt Reynolds was the tension between his affable onscreen persona — the smiling, charming fellow who had major box office hits with crowd-pleasers like “Smokey and the Bandit” and “The Cannonball Run” — and the visible agitation simmering underneath. Reynolds was one of the premier talk show guests (and occasional guest hosts) of the 1970s and early 1980s, a guy who could always be counted on to tell a funny, self-deprecating anecdote that made the audience feel like a part of his inner circle.

But Reynolds always gave the sense that there was a chip on his shoulder — that he was mad about not being taken seriously enough, or being taken too seriously, or losing out on the best parts to his friend and competitor Clint Eastwood and other stars. (Never mind the fact that Reynolds lost out on most of his potentially successful roles — “Terms of Endearment,” “Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman” — because he turned them down, not because anyone took them from him.).

Sources indicate that early on, Eastwood let his controlled rage be a defining trait of his star persona; Reynolds generally tried, and failed, to cloak his under chuckling humility. Many of Reynolds’ best performances exploit this tension, from John Boorman’s “Deliverance,” in which Reynolds’ male bonding fishing expedition descends into a horror, to Paul Thomas Anderson’s “Boogie Nights,” in which the actor’s initially nurturing father figure turns dark and violent when tested.

Reynolds’ memoir, “But Enough About Me,” offers a fascinating glimpse into the contradiction between his healthy self-regard (hilariously exhibited in passages in which he disparages two of the best directors he ever worked with, Anderson and Peter Bogdanovich) and his persistent self-loathing (demonstrated in his candid appraisals of his many terrible personal and professional decisions). The latter informs an ongoing, if intermittent, cycle of Reynolds movies of which “Heat” is a key example: movies I define as “Burt Noir,” in which the actor plays supremely confident men of action tormented by regret and the knowledge that they’ve failed to live up to their potential.

According to recent reports, the first, and possibly best, example of Burt Noir is the 1975 cop drama “Hustle,” in which Reynolds plays a Los Angeles detective surrounded by moral decay and corruption. Reynolds and director Robert Aldrich got to make “Hustle” after their commercial success with “The Longest Yard,” and they immediately squandered whatever mainstream goodwill that comedy had bought them with a film so grim and pessimistic it made James Ellroy look like Fred Rogers.

In “Hustle,” Reynolds is surrounded by evil both banal and terrifying, and he meets almost all of it with a weary resignation — aside from one desperate, possibly pointless act, he doesn’t even try to fight the men to whom he knows he is morally, intellectually, and physically superior. The movie reeks with sadness in spite of being marketed as a muscular action movie — though it is a muscular action movie, as is a later and more commercially successful Burt Noir, “Sharky’s Machine.”.

That movie, in which Reynolds plays a cop who falls for the prostitute he’s got under surveillance, further explores the sense of moral outrage that marked “Hustle” and Reynolds’ directorial debut, “Gator,” and it gives Reynolds another of his tortured heroes who alternates between spurts of violent action and long passages of almost complete impotence — a combination that reaches its apotheosis in “Heat.”.

It has been revealed that A clue to what Reynolds is up to in terms of deconstructing his persona comes in the opening of “Heat,” a 12-minute prologue that doesn’t have much to do with the rest of the film other than breaking down Reynolds’ heroic image for audience members who still see him as a conventional leading man. Reynolds’ Nick Escalante tries to pick up a woman in a bar in the ugliest, aggressive way possible, and it’s confusing for the audience — why has the guy who was such a sweet charmer to Sally Field, Goldie Hawn, Jill Clayburgh, and Julie Andrews in earlier movies turned into such a misogynistic pig?

Sources indicate that even more confusing is what follows, when the meek twerp the woman is dating shows up and beats the hell out of Reynolds in the parking lot. We learn, later on, that the whole thing was a set-up — the guy hired Nick to fake everything so he could look like a hero in front of his girlfriend. But in the audience’s mind, the seed has already been planted; subconsciously we can never quite see this guy as a straightforward hero, and that’s the way Reynolds and screenwriter William Goldman want it.

The film progresses as a kind of hangout movie familiar to anyone who loves Quentin Tarantino’s “Jackie Brown” or “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth”; there’s a relatively solid genre movie structure running underneath everything, but Goldman takes plenty of time for character-developing digressions that give the whole movie a rich sense of melancholy texture.

Escalante’s tale of attempted moral redemption in the form of his efforts to help the victim of a sadistic young gangster avenge her beating moves from sharp wit (in the form of the best dialogue Goldman ever wrote — which is saying something when you’re talking about the guy who wrote “Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid”) and contemplative scenes of self-examination to shocking bursts of expertly choreographed violence and wistful romance.

Sources indicate that it’s all given added layers of irony and resonance by the Las Vegas setting, which seems to mock Escalante’s dreams of hitting it big and escaping to a peaceful retirement in Italy, and Goldman’s choice to set the movie at Christmas, which only mocks Escalante more cruelly. Although “Heat” is one of Goldman’s least well known films (a movie that is easily forgotten amidst the more honored “All the President’s Men,” “Marathon Man,” and “Misery”), it’s one of his most beautifully written, with badinage as snappy as it is revealing and a weaving plot whose emotional effects really sneak up on you.

So why were American critics so dismissive? As is so often the case, they mostly seemed to be reviewing the chaotic circumstances of the production more than the movie that actually resulted from them. “Heat” was a famously troubled movie, whose misfortunes made their way into the press long before the film actually hit American screens. Its beginnings were auspicious: Goldman, one of the most respected writers in the business, was adapting his own novel (with a clause in his contract that said he couldn’t be rewritten), and Robert Altman was set to direct.

Then, only days before shooting, Altman quit the project after his favored cinematographer, Canadian cameraman Pierre Mignot, was denied an H-1 Visa to work in America. Altman claimed that over the course of eight pictures he had developed a style and way of working with Mignot that he didn’t want to abandon, and certainly didn’t want to have to reinvent in a matter of days with another director of photography. Whether or not this is the whole story is anybody’s guess — it was reported that the real reason Altman left had to do with creative differences between him and producer Elliott Kastner, and that Mignot merely gave him the excuse he was looking for to walk.

Sources indicate that goldman suggested Reynolds, who had helmed “Sharky’s Machine” and other fine pictures, take over directing himself, but Burt noted he wanted to focus solely on his performance. Thus began a game of directorial musical chairs that would be widely reported and which gave “Heat” the patina of a disaster in the making. Reliable craftsman Dick Richards came on first, only to leave the production after getting into a fistfight with Reynolds on the set. In spite of lawsuits flying back and forth, Richards returned to the set, only to leave again when he fell off a camera crane and ended up in the hospital.

It has been revealed that on the days when Richards was out second-unit director and stunt coordinator Stan Barrett took on directing duties, and some of the most electrifying moments in “Heat” can be attributed to him. Barrett had worked as Reynolds’ stunt double for more than 20 years and had a great sense of how to capitalize on the actor’s physicality and image, and the set pieces he directed for “Heat” — like a hotel room fight between Reynolds and some thugs — are beautifully staged and filled with brutally effective and original instances of sudden and shocking violence.

Industry observers note that DGA rules at the time prohibited Barrett from taking over the reins for more than five days, since the guild forbade any preexisting member of a troupe from replacing the director — a rule, ironically, that was created when Reynolds’ friend Clint Eastwood fired director Philip Kaufman from “The Outlaw Josey Wales” and replaced him with himself. With only eight days of filming left on “Heat,” television stalwart Jerry Jameson (who had directed Reynolds years earlier on “Dan August”) stepped in and finished the picture.

It has been revealed that the experience doesn’t seem to have been a happy one for many of the principals involved, especially Richards, who gave interviews begging people not to blame him for what he saw as the film’s failures. A DGA arbitration determined that Richards was responsible for 40% of the film — more than any of the other directors on the project — and thus should have the credit. Not wanting his name on the movie, Richards eschewed his usual credit for “Directed by R.M. Richards” and tried to wash his hands of the entire debacle as soon as he could.

With the movie’s own director badmouthing the film in the press, “Heat” never really stood a chance. Yet the movie that exists doesn’t show signs of any of the production’s dysfunction, aside from a slightly abrupt and abbreviated finale (one of several that was shot). In the end, Goldman and Reynolds, more than any director, are the true auteurs of “Heat,” and the consistency of their conception of Nick Escalante as an honorable, self-destructive, romantic, tortured, possibly doomed hero gives “Heat” a lingering emotional resonance and power that still works 40 years later.

According to recent reports, burt would continue his forays into Burt Noir both in film (“Malone,” “Rent-A-Cop,” “Physical Evidence”) and television (“B.L. Stryker,” “Hard Time”), but he never played this kind of character better than he did in “Heat.” The movie was remade, incidentally, in 2015 by “Con Air” director Simon West as “Wild Card.” That version didn’t connect with critics or audiences either, in spite of Goldman once again writing the screenplay. At this point it’s fair to assume that “Heat” is just a doomed project, which is a shame — since it also happens to represent one of Goldman’s finest artistic moments.

  • When it comes to a story as sprawling and complex as "The Lord of the Rings," not all adaptation changes are made equally.
  • While many of the headlines will center on the deception of Charlie Vickers' Sauron and his breakthrough in figuring out how to forge the One Ring, an under-the-radar twist revealed itself all the way in the west on the island kingdom of Númenor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One does not simply walk into spoilers. This article discusses major plot details up to "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 6.

When it comes to a story as sprawling and complex as "The Lord of the Rings," not all adaptation changes are made equally. Throughout three seasons of "The Rings of Power," showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay have given us plenty to choose from. Some, like the arrival of Gandalf (Daniel Weyman), make perfect sense — although technically he's not meant to be involved in the action until centuries later in the timeline, you can understand why the series' creatives would want to speed things up a bit. Others, like the decision to keep Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and her husband Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) apart for so long, took longer to come into focus.

While many of the headlines will center on the deception of Charlie Vickers' Sauron and his breakthrough in figuring out how to forge the One Ring, an under-the-radar twist revealed itself all the way in the west on the island kingdom of Númenor. For several episodes, we've watched rivals and royal cousins Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) and Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) come closer and closer to outright conflict over the throne. How they resolve this may seem to line up with author J.R.R. Tolkien's original telling, but the circumstances vary considerably.

Sources indicate that now we know why the Prime Video series changed things up. In the latest episode, their attempts to negotiate and avoid bloody civil war reach an impasse ... until Pharazôn finds an unexpected solution. Actually, make that a proposal. Yes, this is the moment "The Rings of Power" takes a page out of the "House of the Dragon" playbook. And it could've been much worse.

Sources indicate that "The Lord of the Rings" may have a reputation as cozy, comforting fantasy with its plucky Hobbits and kindly old wizards, but don't look past the abject darkness at the heart of the story. J.R.R. Tolkien never shied away from the shortcomings of individuals throughout his tales — in fact, as a Catholic, he emphasized them. But all it takes is a cursory look at the lore and mythology preceding his most famous novels to realize just how much Middle-earth has in common with the likes of Westeros in "Game of Thrones.".

Recent findings suggest that don't believe us? Look no further than how "The Rings of Power" begins to resolve one of its biggest storylines in Season 3. After several episodes of Númenor coming perilously close to tearing itself apart, we're left on an unsettling cliffhanger. The usurper Pharazôn suggests that he and Míriel repair this rift through an incestuous political marriage. It's clear from the look on Míriel's face that this is a measure of last resort, but everything about her arc thus far implies that she'll end up putting the greater good of the kingdom over her own desires (which, remember, are more romantically inclined towards Lloyd Owen's noble Elendil).

Still, this is far tamer than how Tolkien originally tells it. While the appendices found at the end of "The Return of the King" are light on details, other sources (like "The Silmarillion") explain how Pharazôn looked enviously upon the rightful heir Míriel, forced his cousin into marriage against her will and against all the laws of the land, and took power. Compared to this, "The Rings of Power" gives Míriel far more agency.

In a recent development, those who know their J.R.R. Tolkien ought to be well familiar with where "The Rings of Power" is going next. (For those who don't, be advised this next section dives into major potential spoilers.) With only two episodes to go in Season 3 and the bulk of it likely taking place on the mainland, the Númenor plot will soon need to resolve itself. Míriel must still actually agree to Pharazôn's terms and avoid a costly battle, thus allowing their combined forces to look outwards and send their armada to assist the beleaguered Elves attempting to resist against Sauron.

But it's what comes next, almost certain to unfold in Season 4, that concerns us the most. With their power soon to be consolidated in an uneasy alliance, Míriel and Pharazôn will eventually have to contend with that pesky Dark Lord. According to the various texts, this is the pivotal inflection point that puts us on a path towards the inevitable Fall of Númenor. According to Tolkien's original writings, Númenor's entrance into the war has disastrous consequences. Granted, their fearsome army rapidly overwhelms Sauron's own and leads to him being taken back to the island as a prisoner, but that's where all the troubles begin. Eventually, Sauron worms his way into Pharazôn's ear and convinces him to set his sights on the Valar themselves — a desperate gambit to stave off death among Mortal Men and seize the eternal life that's been denied them.

Industry observers note that none of this ends well for Númenor, but we're getting ahead of ourselves. The final two episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 stream November 25, 2026, on Prime Video.

  • Some are tight, propulsive machines built around a single threat while others sprawl, drift, and gamble on tone, and a few of those gambles are the reason people are still arguing about this show decades later.
  • In a recent development, season six lands at the bottom, and it’s less a failure than a victim of impossible standards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Sopranos is hailed as one of the greatest television shows of all time, known for its impeccable writing, unexpected depth, and unforgettable performances. Created by David Chase, the series follows James Gandolfini as Tony Soprano, a New Jersey mob boss who seeks help from a psychiatrist (Lorraine Bracco) for panic attacks, turning him into a mirror for the audience’s own appetite for violence, loyalty, and self-delusion. Ranking its seasons is a strange, almost unfair exercise because its weakest stretches contain scenes most dramas would kill for: a family dinner gone sour, a dream sequence that unravels a man’s whole life, a road trip to college that turns into a murder. But the seasons are not interchangeable.

Some are tight, propulsive machines built around a single threat while others sprawl, drift, and gamble on tone, and a few of those gambles are the reason people are still arguing about this show decades later. For this ranking, I weighed a few things: how well each season stands on its own as a story, how it deepens Tony and the people orbiting him, the strength of its standout episodes, and how boldly it takes creative risks. Fair warning: the hardest part wasn’t deciding what belongs at the top. It was deciding which brilliant season has to sit at the bottom.

In a recent development, season six lands at the bottom, and it’s less a failure than a victim of impossible standards. Split awkwardly into two parts across more than a year, it never builds the momentum of the tighter seasons before it. Part one is strong, but the season as a whole feels like a show running out of road and losing its focus. Vito Spatafore’s (Joseph R. Gannascoli) storyline, though ambitious, takes up enormous space and ends up feeling disconnected from the rest of the show. A. J. Soprano's (Robert Iler) depression arc is thematically rich, but it often plays out as grim rather than revealing.

Recent findings suggest that another major issue is the overall pacing. Several episodes drift without urgency, and the final nine feel more like a series of elegant gestures than a driving story. Tony’s near-death experience in Atlantic City promises a transformation, but the show quietly retreats from it, leaving his growth stalled. Even the much-debated finale, brilliant as it is, rewards viewers for admiring its ambiguity rather than its payoff and is widely cited as HBO's most controversial ending. Season six has some of the series’ sharpest moments, but when compared with the tension of season one or the tragedy of season five, it simply has less to hold together. Even a weaker season of The Sopranos is better than most demonstrates’ best, but someone has to finish last.

The show's fifth season sits second to last not because it lacks greatness, but because it’s the season most dependent on a single, familiar idea. The season premieres with the return of Tony Soprano’s cousin Tony Blundetto (Steve Buscemi), who is fresh out of prison and determined to go straight, setting up a tragedy that’s easy to see coming. Once he slides back into his former life, the season spends too many episodes waiting for the inevitable. That predictability matters. Earlier seasons kept viewers off balance, but here the central conflict feels more like a slow march than a surprise. Blundetto is compelling, yet he’s also a rerun of the show’s oldest theme: you can’t escape who you are.

Recent findings suggest that the Johnny Sack (Vincent Curatola) and New York storyline adds menace, but it often runs parallel to the main plot rather than driving it. Meanwhile, Carmela’s (Edie Falco) arc, including her entanglement with Furio’s (Federico Castelluccio) absence and her growing resentment, is abundant but occasionally sidelined by the larger crime story. Season five also benefits from its place in the series, which makes its relative weakness feel harsher. Coming after the lean tension of the early years and before the bold stretch to the finish line, it can read as a holding pattern, but episodes such as 'Irregular Around the Margins' and 'The Strong, Silent Type' remain stunning hours of small-screen entertainment.

It has been revealed that season four earns its ranking because it’s the show at its most diffuse. Where earlier seasons organized themselves around a clear antagonist, the fourth season spreads across a looser collection of threads, and the result feels more like a series of vignettes than a single driving story. The central tension, Tony’s feud with Carmine Lupertazzi (Tony Lip) and the New York family over the Esplanade construction deal, simmers but rarely boils. Meanwhile, Ralph Cifaretto’s (Joe Pantoliano) rise and eventual downfall is gripping but resolves mid-season, leaving the back half searching for momentum.

There’s also a restlessness to the season’s mood that is impossible to ignore after a certain amount of time. Moments of deep tragedy, like Adriana La Cerva's (Drea de Matteo) gradual unraveling, share space with oddly broad humor, and the balance doesn’t always land.

According to recent reports, either way, the fourth season still contains episodes like 'Whoever Did This' and 'Whitecaps,' which are considered by many to be some of the most enthralling moments in modern television ever produced. This was a tough choice, but third from the bottom on a show this great is still a high-water mark for almost any other drama.

Sources indicate that season one of The Sopranos takes the third spot because it’s the purest version of what the show set out to do. Thirteen episodes, one clear threat, and no wasted motion. Tony’s war with Uncle Junior (Dominic Chianese) gives the season a spine that later years, for all their ambition, sometimes lack. Every subplot feeds it, from Christopher Moltisanti (Michael Imperioli) and Brendan Filone’s (Anthony De Sando) reckless hijackings to Livia’s (Nancy Marchand) quiet scheming in the background. What lifts it above the weaker seasons is how fully formed the show’s voice already is.

The panic attacks, the therapy sessions with Dr. Melfi, and the tension between family and “the family” arrive with total confidence. Tony is introduced as a man in crisis, not a legend, and that vulnerability gives the violence weight. The season also contains some of the series’ defining hours, notably 'College,' which turns a routine road trip into a masterpiece of dread and marks a major turning point for Gandolfini's character, while 'Isabella' shows the show’s willingness to get strange almost immediately. It stops short of the top two because the stakes, while sharp, are narrower than what came after, but as a debut, it’s nearly flawless. There are very few shows that start this strong, and there are even fewer that still hold up this well on a rewatch.

Season three lands as the show's second runner-up because it may be the series at its most confident, funny, and unsettling all at once. It’s the season where The Sopranos stops proving it can do everything and simply does it. The introduction of Joe Pantoliano's arrival as Ralph Cifaretto gives the season a genuinely terrifying presence as he conveys his character as charming, petty, and capable of sudden cruelty, making it clear that the show has no intention of letting viewers off the hook. Ralph’s volatility pushes Tony into some of his most compromised choices, and his conflict with Tony sharpens the season’s moral stakes.

Meanwhile, the Jackie Aprile Jr. (Jason Cerbone) storyline is a quiet tragedy about inheritance, and Meadow’s (Jamie Lynn-Sigler) role in it adds real emotional cost. Carmela’s arc is richer too, as her loyalty to Tony and her need for something more real pull at her throughout. The season also balances its tone beautifully. Episodes such as 'Employee of the Month' and 'Pine Barrens' show how comfortably the writers could swing between brutality and absurdity, often in the same hour. Dr. Melfi’s storyline gives the season its dramatic center, and the gap between Tony’s therapy and his actions has never been starker. It narrowly misses the top spot only because season two builds a more complete, devastating arc, but season three is the show at full power.

In a recent development, season two takes the top spot because it’s where The Sopranos achieves total control and essentially establishes its intentions. Every thread pulls toward the same devastating destination, and nothing feels wasted. The season’s backbone is Substantial Pussy’s (Vincent Pastore) betrayal, which is a constant source of intensity and uncertainty for fans. Once Tony learns his oldest friend has been wearing a wire, the show builds an agonizing slow burn, and “Funhouse” delivers its payoff as a feverish dream sequence that ranks among the greatest episodes in television history. Tony must kill a man he loves, and the show makes us feel every ounce of that cost.

According to recent reports, around that core, the season layers in Richie Aprile’s (David Proval) volatile return from prison, whose clash with Janice (Aida Turturro) produces both dark comedy and genuine shock. Livia’s death-haunted presence and Junior’s legal troubles keep the family tangled in old grievances, while Christopher’s rise and Adriana’s growing importance give the younger generation real weight. Season two also deepens the show’s central question: can Tony change? His therapy with Dr. Melfi grows more revealing, and “Full Leather Jacket” and “Bust Out” show the cost of the life he has chosen with remarkable economy. It outranks the others because it combines season one’s tight focus with season three’s confidence and adds an emotional gut punch the rest can’t quite match. Season two is not just the best of The Sopranos; it’s a master class in serialized storytelling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upgrade, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it has ended the ground stop.

Sources indicate that on Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:.

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

At this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication complications impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't said what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for users of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

According to recent reports, the controversial author, Rowling, finally published Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone in 1997 after many rejections, and it led to it becoming the biggest book series in history. Since the seven novels concluded, the author has continued writing, whether that be to expand her Harry Potter universe, write other children's novels, write screenplays, or write under pseudonyms to venture into entirely upcoming genres.

Rowling's new crime thriller adaptation is set to be released in one month, just weeks before the upcoming HBO Harry Potter series on December 6. Strike: The Running Grave will return for its seventh season, with Tom Burke back as Detective Cormoran Strike and Holliday Grainger as his partner, Robin Ellacott. It will adapt the seventh novel in Rowling's crime series, written under the pen name Robert Galbraith.

Sources indicate that "When Sir Colin and Sally Edensor approach Cormoran Strike and Robin Ellacott, they are desperate to reconnect with their estranged son, Will. The Edensors enlist the detectives to gather evidence to discredit the Universal Humanitarian Church, a religious cult who have indoctrinated Will and siphoned off his trust fund.".

Recent findings suggest that the seasons include adaptations of The Cuckoo's Calling, The Silkworm, Career of Evil, Lethal White, Troubled Blood, The Ink Black Heart, and now, The Running Grave. The most recent installment of Strike, titled The Ink Black Heart, averaged over 7.1 million viewers, becoming the BBC's most-watched drama.

Burke and Grainger lead a guest cast including James Fleet (known for Bridgerton) as Sir Colin Edensor, Keeley Forsyth (known for Happy Valley) as Mazu Wace and Nichola McAuliffe (known for British soap opera EastEnders) as Shelley Heaton.

The British crime drama Strike first arrived in 2017, and it certainly had a strong reception within the UK before landing on HBO Max in 2021. Season 1, The Cuckoo's Calling, debuted to a strong critical reception and landed an impressive 85% on Rotten Tomatoes. Reviews stated, "It has style and good actors. These days, on television, much depends on the eye of the beholder, this is ever so true with the plot of this series," and "The seven hours are pleasingly old-school, too: no gratuitous violence, a lot of character development and the crimes wrap up like tidy parcels.".

According to recent reports, the news of Strike's return comes after the BBC declared a documentary exploring Rowling and her career, but also the controversial ideals she has been portraying across social media. At the time of writing, there is no official release date.

Industry News: Why the Radical Lesbian Filmmaker Doc ‘Barbara Forever’ Deserves Oscar Recognition

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, finally, a documentary as radical as the lesbian avant-garde feminist filmmaker it’s about.
  • Sources indicate that the documentary, an early fall Strand release produced in partnership with Pamela Koffler and Christine Vachon’s recently Oscar-winning Killer Films, won in Park City for Matt Hixon’s editing.
  • Now Newly introduced York-based, O’Connor centered her George Washington University thesis project on Hammer’s work before they’d ever met.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, finally, a documentary as radical as the lesbian avant-garde feminist filmmaker it’s about. First-time feature filmmaker Brydie O’Connor’s Sundance-winning documentary “Barbara Forever” is a hypnotic archival collage that retraces the life, work, and death of Barbara Hammer.

Sources indicate that the documentary, an early fall Strand release produced in partnership with Pamela Koffler and Christine Vachon’s recently Oscar-winning Killer Films, won in Park City for Matt Hixon’s editing. (Kristen Stewart also jumped on board as an executive producer.) It’s not hard to see why. “Barbara Forever” is an archival documentary that unfolds in the shape and style of its subject, an experimental filmmaker who put together some of the first publicly projected lesbian erotica actually made by a lesbian. Voiceover by the filmmaker spans her early career in the Bay Area (and halcyon days as an out lesbian), her 1992 feature debut “Nitrate Kisses,” and the final years of a cancer battle that ended in 2019. Related Stories Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Substantial Break.

Now Newly introduced York-based, O’Connor centered her George Washington University thesis project on Hammer’s work before they’d ever met. “I read about Barbara and studied Barbara before I even saw her films,” O’Connor told IndieWire. She reached out to Hammer to “buy her DVDs because they weren’t showing anywhere in D.C. And she wrote back to me. At first, she was a little bit hard on me. She was like, ‘I see you’re writing from an edu.edu address. I just want to make sure that you’re actually a student because if you’re faculty, it would be much, much more expensive.’ [Laughs] And I said, ‘I promise, Barbara, I’m a student. I just can’t wait to see your movies.’ And she sent me her DVDs. So yeah, I think that initial impulse to explore her work was really about … ‘Why don’t more people know about Barbara and her work?'”.

Hammer had degrees in psychology and literature before encountering “Meshes of the Afternoon” director Maya Deren’s films (which also influenced David Lynch) at San Francisco State in the 1970s. They lit the fuse for making her own movies. Circa that time, she’d been living in Santa Rosa and married to a man. She came out as a lesbian — busting through that closet, really, with abandon — and took off with her Super 8 camera to start making lesbian films. Growing up in Kansas, O’Connor, in her early 30s, resonated with Hammer’s early biography, and Hammer’s early lust for self-reinvention.

In a recent development, “She was not really tentative about anything. She picked up a camera in her late 20s as she was getting a divorce from a man when she realized that she was a lesbian and she made her film,” O’Connor noted. “She learned by doing. And I was so inspired because, at the time, I was studying American studies and history in school. I had no background in the arts really, except for enjoying consuming them. And I really thought I would be a film critic or a writer… [Barbara Hammer] was not afraid to fail creatively. And she tried so many different ideas, of course, throughout her entire career in making over 85 films, but especially in that first decade of her career.”.

Post-college and in New York, O’Connor, who’s spent “a decade in the Hammer world, and my entire adult consciousness,” would see Hammer at the Metrograph in Lower Manhattan. “I definitely was ‘the girl who wrote her thesis on Barbara,’ probably one of many, and I was day-playing in the film industry,” O’Connor said. “I would occasionally go up to Yale, where her formal archive is held, to continue doing independent research. I was looking at her love letters and her photographs… I wrote to her in January of 2019 when I was about to make my first short film. I said, ‘Hi, Barbara.’ I didn’t know how sick she was at the time. I was like, ‘I’m making my first film. Can I take you to coffee? Do you have any advice for me?’ And she wrote back to me and said, ‘I’m at the very, very end of my life, but best of luck with everything in your career.'”.

Recent findings suggest that hammer died in March 2019, which is when O’Connor contacted the filmmaker’s partner, the human rights advocate Florrie Burke. “Florrie was the love of her life. They were together for 31 years,” O’Connor said. Their meeting culminated in O’Connor’s 2022 short film “Love, Barbara,” which she expanded into the feature that hit theaters this year. In a 2026 Oscar documentary race heavy on genocide and social issues — or a three-hour A24 movie that’s shaken up the entire form — “Barbara Forever” is life-affirming, lovely, yet still-crucial counter-programming.

The organic archival rhythm of “Barbara Forever” eschews talking heads altogether, instead conversing with what Hammer’s work looked and felt like. One of the film’s most charming snippets finds Hammer showing one of her (SFW!) films to a classroom of small schoolchildren. They end up having an unexpected appreciation for the experimental film clip’s non-narrative sensibilities.

O’Connor collaborated with Burke on sifting through 35 hours of audio recordings to stitch together a narration unfolding entirely in Hammer’s own words. “Florrie was so happy with [the short], but she always reminded me there’s so much more to Barbara than just our relationship,” O’Connor said. “Barbara’s this huge personality. She’s so charismatic and charming and really both thoughtful, but also very savvy. She wanted to be recognized. She wanted to be known for her work and her efforts, and she was uncompromising in what she made and how she shared her work. So it just made sense that she would be the narrator of the film.”.

It has been revealed that the Sundance-winning editing, too, proved a challenge, as O’Connor and her filmmaking team pored over more than 400 hours of visual material — from Hammer’s films, to outtakes, B-sides, home videos, and more. “I really wanted to convey with this film: Why did Barbara turn the camera on herself and her life and her lovers and her body as a method of alternative history making? What did she see in the value of that approach and then making experimental cinema out of it and demanding the value of that within culture?”.

That Hammer’s work wasn’t more canonized during her life — an effort O’Connor has made partly her own, especially as a new digital restoration of “Nitrate Kisses” is making the rounds — isn’t only because of how confrontational she was about gender and her own sexuality. “Nitrate Kisses” is, after all, an experimental movie about lesbian repression dating back to the early 20th century. Is it also that autofiction and individualism, now a dominant mode of contemporary artistic expression, were also marginalized at that point within her particular corner of the art world?

Industry observers note that “She was both an experimental filmmaker and avant-garde artist and a lesbian filmmaker. And she indicates, and this was something she said all throughout her life and career, that she didn’t fit neatly into either category where she could just build an audience within that space,” O’Connor said. “She really was uncompromising about being both and working at the intersection of both and having both audiences… The experimental film world didn’t necessarily want to see lesbian work, didn’t necessarily want to see the nude woman’s body on screen. And lesbians, there was not so much representation, especially in the ’70s, ’80s, ’90s, increasingly so, but her work was experimental and thought-provoking, and she felt like a lot of her queer audiences wanted more realistic depictions of queerness.”.

Recent findings suggest that O’Connor, who received a 2026 Creative Capital to not only finish her work on “Barbara Forever” but also continue making docs, said, “The industry is hard, but that certainly won’t stop me from making nonfiction films. I’m just excited to pivot to my next project.”.

“Barbara Forever” is now available to stream on PVOD platforms.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For 17 years, sex-crazed teenagers with a penchant for getting high and/or drunk have had a veritable field day.
  • Horror, Inc., Jason Universe, and Cineverse revealed the news in a press release, which includes the announcement of the new film's final girl, Natalie Alyn Lind as Lauren.
  • The other major announcement is that stunt coordinator Schuyler White will don the hockey mask as Jason Voorhees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For 17 years, sex-crazed teenagers with a penchant for getting high and/or drunk have had a veritable field day. Jason Voorhees, horror's deadliest and most dedicated moralist has been nowhere to be seen. It was starting to look like the only thing that could vanquish Jason for good was a protracted lawsuit, but now, Horror, Inc., which controls the rights to the machete-wielding killer, has moved forward with a new installment titled "Jason." Barring more legal shenanigans, he's set to slay anew on August 13, 2027.

Horror, Inc., Jason Universe, and Cineverse revealed the news in a press release, which includes the announcement of the new film's final girl, Natalie Alyn Lind as Lauren. You might know her from "Dutton Ranch" or the X-Men television series "The Gifted." I find it kinda curious that they're revealing the final girl so far ahead of time. It's typically not hard to identify who's going to be the last girl standing, but there have been some reasonably decent fake-outs in previous movies (I thought Barbara Howard's virginal Sara in "Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter" had a shot at surviving the night). I dunno, maybe they're planning to pull the rug out from under us and kill Lind off early.

The other major announcement is that stunt coordinator Schuyler White will don the hockey mask as Jason Voorhees. Horror, Inc.'s "franchise steward" Robbie Barsamian believes White has the build and presence to be the "most intimidating" Jason ever. Per Barsamian, "[White] approached this theatrical feature like the role of a lifetime, packing 30 pounds of solid muscle onto his 6'5″ frame and studying the iconic Jasons who came before him so that he feels like an unstoppable force of nature." We'll see about that.

Sources indicate that "Jason" wrapped production today after a fairly brief shoot that started in October. It's directed by Steve Miner, who helmed "Friday the 13th Part II" and "Friday the 13th Part III" (in which Jason first slipped on the mask, pictured in the images above). In a recent interview with The Wrap, Barsamian gave fans an idea of what to expect. "This is the scariest and most brutal movie we've ever made," he said. Okay then.

According to recent reports, he went on to say, "We made sure to hold onto all the core elements that make Jason and 'Friday the 13th' what it is. Innovative kills, practical effects, scares and that classic slasher energy, but we really raised the bar across the board. The kills in this film are easily the most creative, brutal, bloody and visceral we've ever done.".

Industry observers note that as for the fresh meat, the probable victims include Matt Corney ("High School Musical: The Musical: The Series") as Asher, Lilia Buckingham ("Hocus Pocus 2") as Madison, John Owen Lowe ("Unstable") as Jake, Summer Madison ("The Summer I Turned Pretty") as Emily, Selena Turner ("Will Trent") as Olive, Matthew Keoni Sato ("High School Musical: The Musical: The Series") as Lucas, Brook Sill ("Stranger Things") as Zoe, Guillermo Diaz ("Scandal") as Rick, Johnell Young ("Wu-Tang: An American Saga") as Frank, Sencere M. Brown ("Homage") as Chase, and Bryan Gael Guzman ("Nickel Boys") as Dylan.

When it comes to raising the bar on kills, I can't help but wonder if they'll try to measure up to the gloriously grotesque mayhem unleashed by Johnny in "In a Violent Nature." Horror fans have become accustomed to latest levels of brutality. We'll see if the old pro Miner can recapture the slasher magic.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when Odysseus (Matt Damon) finally returns home in Homer's Odyssey, he discovers that getting back to Ithaca was only half the battle.
  • Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey brings that showdown to the screen in a climactic fight that required an extraordinary amount of choreography.
  • It has been revealed that speaking with Polygon ahead of the film's home release, Damon and co-star John Leguizamo discussed the sequence, which Leguizamo watched being filmed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when Odysseus (Matt Damon) finally returns home in Homer's Odyssey, he discovers that getting back to Ithaca was only half the battle. His palace has been overrun by suitors hoping to marry his wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), and claim his kingdom. Naturally, Odysseus isn't particularly thrilled about any of this. What follows is one of the epic poem's most memorable confrontations, as the Greek hero takes matters into his own hands.

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey brings that showdown to the screen in a climactic fight that required an extraordinary amount of choreography. But according to Damon, the secret to pulling off the sequence wasn't memorizing a complex choreography. Instead, it was surrounding himself with stunt performers skilled enough to adapt to whatever he did.

It has been revealed that speaking with Polygon ahead of the film's home release, Damon and co-star John Leguizamo discussed the sequence, which Leguizamo watched being filmed. The experience left him wishing he had some popcorn so he could sit back and enjoy the spectacle.

For Leguizamo, watching Damon take on the suitors was one of the production's standout experiences. He even got permission to remove the special contact lenses designed to portray him as the blind swineherd Eumaeus so he could really observe the action. "There were a few times when they'd let me not wear the contacts and just hang out," Leguizamo tells Polygon. "I walked on set when he [Damon] was doing the fight sequences at the end, when he took down all the suitors. That was incredible to watch. It was like watching a Kurosawa samurai movie.".

Leguizamo wasn't part of the fight, but he had a front-row seat as Damon and the stunt team brought the elaborate sequence to life.

According to recent reports, "It was so amazing," Leguizamo continues. "I wanted to have popcorn and just watch it over and over again.".

Industry observers note that the comparison to legendary Japanese filmmaker Akira Kurosawa is particularly fitting given the director's influence on generations of action filmmakers. But Damon is quick to point out that much of the credit should go to the people he was fighting.

"They had the best stunt team," Damon indicates, singling out stunt coordinator George Cottle.

Recent findings suggest that according to Damon, the production benefited from an unusual situation in Los Angeles. With fewer productions underway, highly experienced stunt professionals were available to work on the film, including performers who ordinarily operated at the stunt coordinator level.

Industry observers note that "Because there's not a lot of work in Los Angeles, there were all of these people who were coordinator-level stunt people who were available to come in and play those roles," Damon says. "And a lot of the suitors are around my age. They're older. So these are stunt guys who are incredible, enormously experienced, and really good.".

That experience proved essential once the cameras started rolling. Stunt fighting isn't simply about memorizing a series of punches, blocks, and movements. It's a collaborative process that requires the performers to respond to one another.

"I've always thought stunt fighting is like dancing, really," Damon says. He also acknowledges that he wasn't necessarily the most accomplished dancer in the group. "When one, me, isn't as good a dancer, it gets made up for by the other being an expert.".

Rather than expecting Damon to execute every movement with the precision of a professional stunt performer, the team could adjust its timing and positioning around him.

Sources indicate that "I could move through these sequences, because these guys were adjusting in real time to my movement and my spacing," Damon indicates. "And if I was off, they could recalibrate and still make it work.".

That level of experience was especially important given the sheer amount of choreography involved.

Recent findings suggest that "How many moves did you have? Did you count them?" Leguizamo asks.

It has been revealed that "I have no idea," Damon replies. "It was a lot. It was hundreds of moves.".

"They must have been over a hundred," Leguizamo agrees.

Sources indicate that "These guys were just so great," Damon concludes. "That really made that sequence what it was.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, "The Terminator" bowed in 1984 but was so ahead of its time it could easily debut today and be just as, if not more relevant. The film's encapsulation of society's collective fear of a technological future gave what would have otherwise been a sci-fi slasher B-movie real depth. Paired with James Cameron's still-developing yet impressive filmmaking skills, honed over years spent toiling for Roger Corman's Upcoming World Pictures and a particularly unfortunate experience on 1982's "Piranha II: The Spawning," that remarkable prescience made the film an instant classic that also happened to give its star, Arnold Schwarzenegger, his most memorable catchphrase.

According to recent reports, long before 2019's "Terminator: Dark Fate" made Schwarzenegger give up on the franchise altogether, Cameron's original masterpiece combined elements of the burgeoning slasher genre with sci-fi and action spectacle to create a truly original moviegoing experience (even if the insatiably litigious Harlan Ellison claimed "The Terminator" was all his idea). The fact that any movie gets produced is a marvel in its own way, but "The Terminator" was a real miracle, wrought by the sheer will of its director and his producing partner Gale Anne Hurd to actually get the film made. Their persistence paid off. What could have easily been an overlooked low-budget sci-fi actioner became a modest sensation, making $78.4 million on a $6.4 million budget and launching Cameron's career.

It has been revealed that clearly, the writer/director had tapped into something larger with his story of a murderous cyborg sent back through time to kill the woman who would birth the leader of the human resistance. Audiences were enraptured and 42 years later the movie remains just as chillingly pertinent and wildly entertaining as it was in the mid-'80s. As such, Arnie's most famous line arguably remains the greatest sci-fi quote of all time.

Arnold Schwarzenegger initially had no interest in "The Terminator, which considering this film (alongside his lead performance in 1982's "Conan the Barbarian") turned him into a movie star is hard to believe. Similarly, the Austrian Oak was reluctant to deliver what has since become the movie's most memorable line. Thankfully, James Cameron won him over.

The scene in question sees Arnie's Terminator arrive at a police station in search of Linda Hamilton's Sarah Connor. There, he's told by the officer on duty to take a seat and wait. Substantial mistake. Presumably, this unstoppable killer robot could have just punched his way through the glass facade between him and the officer before rampaging through the station to find his target. But that's no fun. Instead, Cameron — who would later jump a semi-truck into a Los Angeles viaduct in "Terminator 2: Judgment Day" — decided to have Arnie's robot ram a sedan through the doors of the station and into the reception desk, pinning the officer to the wall. Before he does so, however, the Terminator says the line.

Sources indicate that after the officer tells him to take a seat, Schwarzenegger calmly takes a look around, leans in and indicates three words: "I'll be back." Of course, he's referring to the fact he'll soon ram the policeman between a wall and a car. But like the movie in which they're spoken, the words proved to be oddly prophetic. The Terminator did return, multiple times. Only the aforementioned "T2" lived up to the original, but the simple phrase, "I'll be back," almost came to represent the way in which "The Terminator" and its sequel remain perennially relevant as we hurtle towards the AI-driven garbage future that awaits.

"Come with me if you want to live.".

Recent findings suggest that "That Terminator is out there. It can't be bargained with. It can't be reasoned with. It doesn't feel pity, or remorse, or fear. And it absolutely will not stop, ever, until you are dead!".

Industry observers note that "You still don't get it, do you? He'll find her! That's what he does! That's all he does! You can't stop him! He'll wade through you, reach down her throat, and pull her f****** heart out!".

It has been revealed that "Your son gave me a message to give to you. He made me memorize it. 'Thank you, Sarah, for your courage through the dark years. I can't help you with what you must soon face except to say that the future is not set. You must be stronger than you imagine you can be. You must survive or I will never exist.' That's all.".

"Your clothes, give them to me, now.".

#4712. 10 Classic Sci-Fi Shows That Are Better Than Modern Streaming Originals

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1543 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Collider ↗ Open Full Page

10 Classic Sci-Fi Shows That Are Better Than Modern Streaming Originals

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's nothing quite like the classics.
  • Recent findings suggest that for the purposes of this list, any show that began before the advent of streaming in the 2010s, and which never became a streaming show (which discounts gems like Black Mirror and Futurama), will be considered a potential classic.
  • While working on the spy series Danger Man, Patrick McGoohan and George Markstein came up with the idea for The Prisoner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's nothing quite like the classics. As the streaming era has led television as a whole to evolve in ways nobody could have predicted a couple of decades ago, so too has small-screen science fiction transformed in several ways, leaving behind the days of classic sci-fi TV. But as powerful, high-quality, and undeniably cinematic as many sci-fi indicates from the streaming era are, there are several classics which are simply unbeatable.

Recent findings suggest that for the purposes of this list, any show that began before the advent of streaming in the 2010s, and which never became a streaming show (which discounts gems like Black Mirror and Futurama), will be considered a potential classic. However, age is only the first step. A true sci-fi classic is that which has had a great impact and influence on the genre, one so great and so pop-culturally relevant that it can be considered a must-see.

While working on the spy series Danger Man, Patrick McGoohan and George Markstein came up with the idea for The Prisoner. It's widely disputed whether McGoohan is the show's primary creator or the pair share true co-creator status, but one thing remains certain: This is one of those near-perfect sci-fi demonstrates that nobody remembers anymore, a testament to the genius of British sci-fi storytelling.

Industry observers note that praised for its psychological depth, surreal brilliance, and avant-garde sensibilities, The Prisoner was absolutely revolutionary back in the '60s, pioneering auteur-driven television decades before it became the norm. It's both a deep countercultural allegory and one of the most entertaining sci-fi spy shows ever made, with a cryptic series finale that's among the most memorable in the genre's history.

After a brainstorming session at a Comic-Con while they were working on 2009's Star Trek, J. J. Abrams, Roberto Orci, and Alex Kurtzman came up with the idea for Fringe, one of the best spooky cop shows of all time. What started out as more of an episodic procedural inspired by the likes of The X-Files and The Twilight Zone soon turned into something far more serialized and creative.

According to recent reports, the show knew exactly how to take full advantage of the constraints of network television in all the best ways, and it constantly demonstrated that mastery throughout its run. Instead of a regular "monster-of-the-week" procedural that might have gotten buried after a couple of seasons, Fringe proved that mysteries which seemed to be standalones could actually lay down the foundations for a much richer, more engaging multiverse.

After the success of Roland Emmerich's 1994 film Stargate, a franchise of the same title was introduced forward, peaking just three years later. Indeed, Stargate SG-1 is not only the best installment in the whole franchise, but truly one of the greatest sci-fi reveals of the network TV era. Spanning over 200 episodes, it took the film's high-concept premise and transformed it into a sprawling, timeless saga.

It's one of those sci-fi reveals that shouldn't be remade, because how could you possibly top perfection? Stargate SG-1 still does everything right nearly two decades after its conclusion, from relying on a phenomenal cast playing some deeply engaging characters to a perfect blend between high-stakes drama and self-aware humor. The reason why it managed to run for a whopping 10 years is that it's among the most widely accessible sci-fi shows in history.

Cowboy Bebop is widely considered one of the biggest landmarks in the history of anime television, having fundamentally changed how global audiences and creators themselves viewed Japanese animation the world over. Never before had the world seen such a genre-bending and cinematic anime show, and rarely had the Western world fallen so deeply in love with a series like this.

It's one of the truest masterpieces of '90s anime television, a space Western with neo-noir tinges that's still just as stylish and universally entertaining today as it was decades ago. Generally considered one of the best gateway series for people who have never watched anime before, it's a visually stunning masterpiece with some of the best direction, writing, music, and voice acting that the medium has ever seen.

According to recent reports, there are plenty of classic sci-fi demonstrates that are better than most newly introduced series, and Babylon 5 is both one of the most noteworthy and one of the most massively influential. Quite unprecedented for American network television at the time, this space opera was written as a kind of novel for television, where each season was designed to serve as a new chapter in that story.

It's not like the small screen had never seen serialization before, but never before had sci-fi television seen serialization on this scale. Decades later, Babylon 5 still feels every bit as fresh and exciting as it did when it was originally on the air, and the technical elements that may look a bit dated only further add to its timeless charm. Without Babylon 5, sci-fi television as a whole wouldn't be what it is today.

There are plenty of sci-fi shows that have been canceled after only one short-lived season throughout the years, unable to reach their full potential — but none nearly as notorious or iconic as the space Western cult classic Firefly. It's one of the most perfect sci-fi shows of the last 25 years, one so great that one season was all it took for it to become one of the biggest sci-fi cult classics in the history of 21st-century television.

It was due to missteps unique to the network era of television, like airing episodes out of order, that Firefly didn't get to flourish, which only makes it even more of a crucial piece of network sci-fi television history. With its perfect blend of Americana aesthetics and fun sci-fi pulp, a delectably compelling ensemble of characters, and plenty of razor-sharp dialogue, it's no wonder why Firefly is as legendary as it is.

First airing in 1966, Star Trek: The Original Series proved that far from just being a source of pulpy entertainment, sci-fi could be a true mirror for contemporary social and political complications. Star Trek: The Next Generation grabbed that thematic thesis and carried it forward to lengths never seen before, delivering what many fans still agree is the best piece of Star Trek content to date.

Recent findings suggest that with a top-tier cast led by the late Sir Patrick Stewart, some incredible production values, and some of the most profound and philosophically charged writing the genre has ever seen, The Next Generation is one of those space sci-fi shows that are genuine masterpieces. It's the space opera subgenre at its most optimistic and complex, and a must-see for anyone who even slightly enjoys network television sci-fi.

The original Battlestar Galactica from 1979 is still delightfully charming today, but it was seriously in need of an enhancement. After several attempts to make either a sequel or a reboot, the series was finally born anew with the 2003 miniseries of the same name, which was followed by the full-length 2004 show that is nowadays remembered as one of the best sci-fi reveals of the 21st century.

In a recent development, indeed, Battlestar Galactica is one of those mega-addictive sci-fi reveals that are impossible to stop watching, an absolutely legendary space opera that completely changed how broadcast science fiction looked, sounded, and felt. Rusty, gritty, and written as a thematic response to the national mood of the media following the 9/11 attacks, it's one of the most complex and well-written sci-fi shows of all time.

It has been revealed that one of the most fun TV indicates of the 1990s, The X-Files was a watershed moment in the history of broadcast television, pioneering the very concept of online fandom. To this day, its fans are still some of the most loyal and dedicated in the history of sci-fi television, and that's because this iconic show was so perfectly designed to endure the test of time.

Recent findings suggest that two FBI Special Agents solving mysteries together; one a fierce believer in the supernatural, the other a skeptic. It's a simple enough concept to base a sci-fi show on, but it's admirable just how long X-Files made that concept last. It's the gold standard for sci-fi procedurals, a real masterpiece of television's network era that always knew exactly how much serialization to inject into its episodic nature.

If there is any one show that deserves to be called the most influential in the history of sci-fi television, it's undoubtedly Rod Serling's The Twilight Zone, the greatest and most notable anthology TV series of all time. Full of incredible stars, plenty of stellar writing, and some of the most genius high-concept premises in all of sci-fi television, it's a must-see classic without equal.

Like all anthology series, The Twilight Zone certainly had its highs and lows over the course of its run, but every single one of its seasons could reasonably be counted among the best anthology TV seasons of all time. It's the closest that sci-fi TV ever came to perfection throughout the entirety of the broadcasting era of the medium, and it will take something really special to ever top it during this new streaming era.
