📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers are never late, nor are they early, but arrive precisely when they mean to. This article discusses major plot details from "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 Episodes 5-6.

Ages may pass, tyrants come and go, but some things in Middle-earth never change. As we reach the endgame of "The Rings of Power" Season 3, the Prime Video series is approaching the halfway point of its five-season initiative. Although this takes place thousands of years before the events of "The Lord of the Rings," this inevitably means that Middle-earth is beginning to look much like the version we remember from Peter Jackson's spiritually-related (though canonically separate) films.

Industry observers note that the looming threat of Charlie Vickers' Sauron is the most obvious link between the Second and Third Ages of J.R.R. Tolkien's fantasy epic, of course, but the similarities extend far beyond the self-styled Lord of the Rings. The various peoples of the land still profoundly distrust each other despite their common enemy, Ringwraiths are on the prowl, and everything's building to the forging of the One Ring to rule them all. But don't look past one of the most surprising developments of all: the brewing rivalry between Daniel Weyman's Gandalf and the so-called Dark Wizard Pallando (Ciarán Hinds).

In Episode 3, we learned that Gandalf's purpose was to save Pallando rather than defeat him, but our Grey wizard swiftly finds this easier said than done. Pallando the Blue has found himself backed into a corner, caught between a Nazgnagôl and a Dark Lord. And no matter how much Gandalf urges him to join their power together and unite against their foe, the Dark Wizard's actions in Episode 5 give us a wizard-on-wizard fight that feels like a remake of Gandalf's struggles with Saruman centuries later.

As a certain "Star Wars" director once so memorably put it, "It's like poetry, sort of. They rhyme." Obviously, George Lucas was trying to verbalize the idea of mythology and lore echoing through the ages — humans love ourselves some cyclical storytelling, after all. "The Lord of the Rings" is no different. In this case, "The Rings of Power" has the added challenge of having to live in the shadow of an all-timer trilogy and contend with an audience that has come to view those movies as the definitive version of this story.

Well, if you can't beat 'em, join 'em. Showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay opted for a trip down memory lane with Gandalf and Pallando's long-awaited reunion after Season 2. Burdened with the glorious purpose of redeeming his fellow wizard (as handed down by the Secret Fire), Gandalf tries to reason with the Dark Wizard ... before things ultimately turn violent. Between Pallando's entreaties that they must "kneel" to Sauron and the subsequent duel with their magical staffs, it's all very reminiscent of a similar moment in "The Fellowship of the Ring." While visiting his "old friend," Gandalf realizes to his horror that the great wizard Saruman (Christopher Lee) is now in thrall to Sauron and now urges Gandalf to "join" him.

From the dialogue to the fight choreography to Bear McCreary's score, this sequence clearly attempts to evoke the Saruman/Gandalf dynamic for viewers. But, rather than serve as a mere reference for the sake of it, this actually helps make this battle more meaningful. Down the line, hundreds and hundreds of years in the future, we can imagine an older and wiser Gandalf remembering this encounter with Pallando when he visits Saruman.

What's a magical wizard's duel or two between very old friends? As Gandalf learns early on in "The Rings of Power" Season 3, the all-powerful godlike being known as Eru Ilúvatar sent five wizards (known as Istari) to Middle-earth. In the official canon laid down by J.R.R. Tolkien, this occurred early in the Third Age — the same time period that the events of "The Lord of the Rings" take place in — as a way to bring aid during Sauron's latest return. In "The Rings of Power," this has been moved up to the Second Age and it's easy to see why. As a result, the creative team can now use this meeting between Gandalf and Pallando (which doesn't take place in any of Tolkien's texts) to reflect and echo his later experience with Saruman.

It's a neat, ironic twist that this happens to involve a Dark Wizard whom many fans once thought might be Saruman himself. Instead, Episode 5 uses Pallando the Blue as a parallel to Saruman the White's eerily similar fall into darkness. Since this subplot is entirely missing from Episode 6, we'll have to wait and see how Episode 7 and the finale wrap things up — whether Gandalf proves successful in his mission to win Pallando back from the clutches of evil, or if Pallando's mysterious vision from the Secret Fire proves true and his doom really does come at the hands of "a ring-bearer" as he foresaw.

Sources indicate that either way, this lends all sorts of weight to Gandalf's later struggle with Saruman. Seeing one wizarding friend turn to the dark side is bad enough, but reliving it all over again? That's some serious trauma.

Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let customers scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers.
  • Google indicates it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for people whose data was found on the dark web.
  • Sources indicate that dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let customers scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the organization discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with new scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

Google indicates it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for people whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a new service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

Sources indicate that dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google rolled out the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One consumers, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

Sources indicate that you'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

It’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

Sources indicate that but perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that users want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the company hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

It has been revealed that many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

There isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

If your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

Finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

The latest "Hunger Games" film, "Sunrise on the Reaping," is arguably the bleakest and meanest entry in the franchise yet. The "Hunger Games" equivalent of the fantastic "Star Wars" series "Andor," it tells a devastating tale about loss, sacrifice, and people who don't know if they'll ever get to see victory or freedom. As /Film's review puts it, "Beyond the shock value, this story remains human, emotional, and gripping from beginning to end.".

Sources indicate that at the same time, "Sunrise on the Reaping" is very much a prequel. In addition to its many callbacks to previous "Hunger Games" movies (including 2023's "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes"), it's full of younger versions of well-known characters like Effie Trinket and Caesar Flickerman (as played here by Elle Fanning and Kieran Culkin, respectively). But above all else, it's a story that reveals how a young Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) survived his own horrifying set of Games.

Joining Haymitch on his journey are his fellow District 12 tributes, among them Ben Wang as Wyatt Callow. Wang, as it were, has quickly made a name for himself, appearing in everything from the sequel "Karate Kid: Legends" to the devastating Stephen King adaptation "The Long Walk" (as was directed by longtime "Hunger Games" helmsman Francis Lawrence). And by the look of things, the actor's career will only continue to flourish in the near-future.

Industry observers note that after scoring a small part in an episode of the "MacGyver" reboot series, Ben Wang landed the lead role in the short-lived but well-received Disney+ series "American Born Chinese" (which has some very cool action scenes and a killer cast). Around that same time, he also appeared in the feature film adaptation of the "Mean Girls" stage musical.

It has been revealed that still, it was really the one-two punch of 2025's "Karate Kid: Legends" (pun kinda intended) and "The Long Walk" that proved Wang could be a star. The former, in particular, demonstrated the young actor could go toe to toe with "Karate Kid" franchise veterans Ralph Macchio and Jackie Chan while still shining on his own merits. What's more, it allowed him to earn his action movie bonafides, as he does more than his fair share of convincing stunt work in the film.

Then came the emotionally obliterating all-time great Stephen King adaptation that is "The Long Walk," in which Wang delivers a harrowing and heart-wrenching performance — making it the perfect prelude to his turn in "Sunrise on the Reaping." And while there's not much action in the movie, it's an equally dark dystopian work in which kids compete to the death to try and better their lots in life.

In a recent development, ultimately, Wang doesn't have a huge role in "Sunrise on the Reaping," but he makes the most of his screen time, depicting Wyatt as an oddsmaker desperate to demonstrate he can control his own life and beat the odds in the games. Up next, the actor will co-star in the sixth and final season of Apple TV's acclaimed sci-fi series "For All Mankind" before joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe as Iceman in a upcoming "X-Men" film.

GTA 6 Learned All the Right Lessons From Zelda: Breath of the Wild

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that throwing players into an open-world game can be challenging.
  • In GTA 6, you don’t start your life of crime in the heart of Vice City.
  • It has been revealed that for those unfamiliar with Florida, the Leonida Keys are a near-perfect representation of the real-life Florida Keys.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that throwing players into an open-world game can be challenging. When your game has an enormous map, you risk giving players almost too much freedom up front. There’s a very careful art in helping players get acclimated to how exploration works in a game without totally restricting any sense of exploration. The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild famously nailed the art of an open-world introduction in 2017 with its meticulously crafted starting area, the Great Plateau. Now, nearly a decade later, Grand Theft Auto 6 has pulled off the same trick.

In GTA 6, you don’t start your life of crime in the heart of Vice City. In fact, it can take up to 20 hours to get there if you’re focused on the story. Instead, the entire first chapter takes place in the southernmost part of its map, the Leonida Keys. It’s a series of small, isolated islands where Jason has holed up in a dilapidated shack.

It has been revealed that for those unfamiliar with Florida, the Leonida Keys are a near-perfect representation of the real-life Florida Keys. The islands, in reality, are narrow stretches of land chained together by bridges. Since you’re close to the water no matter where you are, most of the houses in the area are built on tall stilts to account for flooding. The Keys are densely packed with buildings, but on very limited patches of land, an approach to urban planning that can make them feel a little removed from reality. I was down in the Keys for a wedding a few years ago, and I couldn’t stop wondering what someone would do if they had an emergency and needed to get to the one nearby hospital during a single-lane traffic jam. It’s a truly unique place in America, which makes it a perfect locale for a series that’s obsessed with eccentric corners of the country.

Sources indicate that but more than that, the layout of the Leonida Keys perfectly lends itself to a great open-world introduction. Key Lento, where you’ll spend most of your time in the early hours of GTA 6, is a thin town that feels about as substantial as a Like a Dragon map. Even though it’s not a huge space that’s lined with clubs, it still includes everything you need to get a feel for Leonida’s wider design. There’s a central highway that runs through the middle, giving you a place to zip through town while learning traffic laws. There are enough roadside shops to teach you how to buy guns, food, clothing, and more. On the edges of all that, you have your suburban side roads. And then you have shores on all sides, giving you easy access to the water for some early game fishing and diving.

According to recent reports, basically, you’ll learn all the basics you need to know about moving through Leonida in that compact space. You’ll be able to do that without getting pulled into too many distractions that take you far from home, as there’s only one way in and out of town. On the flipside, there’s still enough to discover in Key Lento that it doesn’t feel like you’re on a leash. Even when I went back to Key Lento after 60 hours, I found a hidden car livery in a garage I’d passed many times. You could easily spend the length of a normal GTA campaign just seeing it all in Chapter 1.

In a weird way, the Leonida Keys’ perfect design brings me back to the Great Plateau. Nintendo had a difficult task on its hand when it decided to turn Zelda into an open-world game with Breath of the Wild. How do you adapt the basic principles of the series, especially its precise tool-based puzzle-solving, into a version of Hyrule that you can explore freely? The solution was to ease players in with a controlled tutorial zone. When you zoom out and consider it in context of the full map, the Great Plateau is miniscule. It only has a few points of interest, and a handful of items to collect and wandering monsters to fight.

The magic of it, though, is that it never actually feels small. For players coming to an open-world Zelda game for the first time, it felt revelatory. It didn’t even feel like you were being subjected to a very well-designed set of tutorials. There was so much to see and do! It was only once you glided off the Plateau that you realized that you had only seen a tiny fraction of Hyrule, a revelation that made the true open-world reveal that much more impressive. And once you got there, you had all the tools and knowledge you needed to start climbing cliffs, seeking out shrines, and hunting for Koroks. The rest of the game comes from the mounting complexity of how those tools are used to solve trickier puzzles, a design philosophy that has cemented the Great Plateau in history as one of gaming’s most beloved introductions.

It has been revealed that everything that works about the Great Plateau in Breath of the Wild hit me when I explored the Leonida Keys in GTA 6. It provided a natural playground where I could learn the ropes before reaching the mainland and having my attention pulled in all directions. By the time I finally got to Vice City, I actually came to miss how serene and compact it all was compared to the bustle of city life. I still find myself driving back down there once and a while just to check in on my old neighbors or go on a little fishing expedition. (Okay, and also to rob a local bank, sue me.) After touring an entire state, Key Lento still feels like home for Jason.

Tendo Nagenda, a former executive on Netflix’s film team, has been tapped as president of Proximity Media, the production firm founded by Ryan Coogler, Zinzi Coogler, and Sev Ohanian, the founders revealed Thursday.

Nagenda spent four years at Netflix under film chief Scott Stuber, exiting in 2022, and in that time he shepherded films like Spike Lee’s “Da 5 Bloods,” “The Old Guard,” “Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom,” “The Harder They Fall,” and “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery.”.

Nagenda will oversee all aspects of creative development and production at Proximity, including its film, TV, and non-fiction divisions, and will report directly to the founders. The heads of Film, Television and Nonfiction will all report directly to Nagenda, and he’ll work alongside marketing and operations lead Terra Potts and music lead Ludwig Göransson. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Apple first announced Face ID, the firm talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.
  • Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security ….
  • The first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Apple first announced Face ID, the firm talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.

Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security ….

The first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011. This didn’t include any extra hardware, simply using the front-facing camera to take a photo and compare this to a stored image of the user.

It took just days to discover just how insecure this approach is, with unlock achieved simply by holding up a photo of the owner’s face on another device. Yet even as late as 2019, Samsung was continuing to use this approach.

According to recent reports, meantime, in 2017 Apple rolled out Face ID in the iPhone X. This has an entire hardware module devoted to it, with infrared emitters and receivers used to create a 3D map of the shape of our face. This cannot be fooled by photos or even models, and Apple remarked at the time there was a less than a one in a million chance of it being fooled (with riders for twins, etc).

Industry observers note that face ID projects more than 30,000 invisible IR dots. The IR image and dot pattern are pushed through neural networks to create a mathematical model of your face and send the data to the secure enclave to confirm a match, while adapting to physical changes in appearance over time. All saved facial information is protected by the secure enclave to keep data extremely secure, while all of the processing is done on-device […] The probability that a random person in the population could look at your iPhone or iPad Pro and unlock it using Face ID is less than 1 in 1,000,000.

Given the massive contrast in security of the two approaches, it might seem odd that Apple is now adapting a purely visual face unlock feature. The only reason the tech giant is doing this is because the lack of Face ID has been far and away one of the biggest complaints about the iPhone Duo.

I suspect Apple made the decision reluctantly and over the protests of security engineers. But while face unlock remains a very insecure approach compared to Face ID, Apple’s approach tries to strike a good balance between convenience and security. The following safeguards apply:.

That latter restriction means it can’t be used for Apple Pay, to unlock password-protected apps, to open the Passwords app, or to do anything else that requires authentication – such as changing your passcode or adding a fingerprint to Touch ID.

In a recent development, I do not see any downside provided the feature is off by default and only those who want it will turn it on. Presumably with an explanation of the reasons it gives reduced security.

For myself, I have got so used to using touch ID on my keyboard that I'd likely not make use of it in my business. If anything goes wrong with client information, I want to know, and be able to demonstrate, that I have taken security seriously.

There’s only one other safeguard I’d like to see Apple introduce: geolocking. Personally, I’d want to be able to allow face unlock at home, but disable it when I’m out and about. At the moment, the only two ways to temporarily disable it are to toggle it off or to restart the phone. I’d like to see an option to set safe locations, like home and work, with the feature disabled in public.

Given that Face unlock requires only a front-facing camera, there’s absolutely no reason why Apple couldn’t also make it available on the Mac.

Face ID has been something MacBook users have been wanting for a great many years, and despite a decade’s worth of Apple patents for just this, it still hasn’t happened. Face unlock would be a compromise option that would at least get us some of the way there. I see I’m not the first to suggest this, with Macworld’s Roman Loyola beating me to it.

What’s your view? If you own an iPhone Duo, will you choose to enable this? If you own a MacBook, would you like the same option on that? Please take our poll and share your thoughts in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers ahead for Episodes 5 and 6 of "The Rings of Power" Season 3.

According to recent reports, as a "Lord of the Rings" prequel, "The Rings of Power" takes an interesting approach. Sure, when you think about it, the show doesn't always fit into he greater "Lord of the Rings" canon, and it sometimes introduces elements that threaten to change the larger franchise as we know it. At the same time, it has some pretty cool ideas, whether it's the creation of Mount Doom from Season 1 or Sauron (Charlie Vickers) meeting a Balrog (Simon Pegg) in Season 3. Overall, the series knows how to capitalize on the vastness of J. R. R. Tolkien's literary source material to imagine fresh concepts for a different medium.

Recent findings suggest that but perhaps one of the most fascinating aspects of "The Rings of Power" is how its writers have been able to reference material from "The Silmarillion" — in particular, where it concerns the First Age of Middle-earth — despite Amazon not having the rights to adapt the book. Not only that, the show has alluded to plot points from that work on more than one occasion, be it Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) being jealous that he's unable to match the craft of the legendary Fëanor or the continuous allusions to Morgoth being Sauron's former boss.

In a recent development, "The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 5 even name-drops a First Age legend when Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) tells Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) exactly how he was captured so many centuries ago. As it turns out, he was taken in after Ancalagon the Black — the most powerful dragon in Middle-earth's history — set his entire legion ablaze, with Sauron astride. The only reason Celeborn survived was because he was kicked off his horse and into some water, shielding him from the inferno.

Ancalagon the Black has never appeared on-screen, but his legacy is legendary. In J.R.R. Tolkien's literature, dragons were specifically bred by Morgoth, first as terrestrial lizards, but later as winged monsters. Ancalagon was known as the Great Dragon of Morgoth, the largest winged dragon in the history of Middle-Earth. He is described by Tolkien as being "as tall as a mountain" and was the leader of the great host of winged dragons that Morgoth unleashed during the War of Wrath in the First Age. The great beast only serves one purpose in the larger Legendarium — to be Morgoth's ultimate weapon of war, one so terrible it nearly ruined the Valar.

In a recent development, ancalagon is by far the largest dragon in fiction and is much, much larger than any of the dragons in George R.R. Martin's "Game of Thrones" stories, the massive Balerion the Dread included. But unlike Balerion, Ancalagon didn't really do much. Indeed, in Tolkien's canon, he basically appeared for about a day, driving back the Valar until Eärendil arrived with his flying ship and an army of eagles led by their king, Thorondor. Eärendil and the eagles then battled Ancalagon and the dragons for a day and night, only for Eärendil to eventually overthrow the great dragon and cast him into the volcanoes of Thangorodrim (where Morgoth's fortress lay).

Recent findings suggest that the death of Ancalagon also marked the end of the War of Wrath in Middle-earth. And even though the race survived, as evidenced by the later existence of dragons like Smaug, they never reached the heights of the Great Dragon again. Anyway, there's something for you to keep in your back pocket as you continue making your way through "The Rings of Power" on Prime Video.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't train for the Hunger Games if you haven't seen "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" or the original set of "Hunger Games" films — spoilers ahead!

Suzanne Collins, the author of the "Hunger Games" books, doesn't reliably write upcoming stories set within this expansive, totalitarian universe. 10 years after the final novel in her original trilogy, "Mockingjay," hit shelves, she decided to write "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," a prequel that brings us back to some of Panem's earliest days. Similarly, her 2025 book "Sunrise on the Reaping" looks at the 50th Hunger Games.

Recent findings suggest that so, how does the "Hunger Games" timeline even work at this point? It's actually still pretty streamlined, even with Collins jumping around in mentioned timeline across various books. With that in mind, let me walk you through it.

We'll return to "Ballad" and the original trilogy in a moment (all of which have blockbuster movie adaptations, obviously), but as for "Sunrise on the Reaping," the film version stars Joseph Zada as young Hunger Games victor Haymitch Abernathy and sits smack in the middle between "Ballad" and the very first "Hunger Games" book and movie. During the 50th Games (which, as the second "Quarter Quell" — meaning, an extra-evil edition of the Games held every 25 years — features 48 teenage tributes fighting to the death on TV instead of 24), Haymitch makes crucial alliances, defies the odds, and emerges as the winner. Decades later, he serves as a mentor to characters we meet in "The Hunger Games," making "Sunrise on the Reaping" an important bridge between "Ballad" and the other "Hunger Games" stories.

(A note: specific years are never mentioned in the franchise, so we just use iterations of the Games to organize its timeline.).

In 2020, Suzanne Collins released "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" (her first "Hunger Games" book in a decade), and it focused on the 10th Hunger Games and a young Coriolanus Snow, the man who grows up to be the oppressive president of the totalitarian dystopia known as Panem. In both the book and its film adaptation (where Coriolanus, or "Coryo," is played by Tom Blyth), we meet Coryo as his family faces poverty, total reputational ruin, and even eviction from their home in the Capitol. Desperate to claw his way back up the ladder (his family has a saying that "snow lands on top"), Coryo decides that the tribute he mentors must win the 10th Games, which are newly televised and which take place in a downtrodden, themeless arena (something that changes quite a bit as the Games continue).

Industry observers note that unfortunately for Coryo, his dean at the Capitol Academy, Casca Highbottom (Peter Dinklage), hated Coryo's deceased dad and gives him a tribute from the impoverished coal mining district, 12, assuming she can't possibly win. That, admittedly, backfires: Songstress Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler) from the musical Covey not only charms viewers watching the Games at home, but Coryo himself, and he helps her cheat and win the Games.

Sources indicate that when Coryo's machinations are discovered, he's sent to become a Peacekeeper in District 12 ... and despite reuniting with Lucy Gray there, he keeps secrets that send her fleeing, and his descent into depravity truly begins. We do see Snow in "Sunrise on the Reaping" (as president and played by Ralph Fiennes in the movie adaptation), and appropriately, he warns Haymitch about girls from the Covey after learning about his Covey girlfriend and Lucy Gray's descendant, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak).

According to recent reports, president Snow is still Panem's leader by the time we get to "The Hunger Games" and are introduced to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), the girl and boy chosen to represent District 12 in the 74th annual Hunger Games. Haymitch, portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the original films, is their mentor, and he initially phones it in after years of mentoring young tributes only to watch them die on TV in variously horrifying ways. He does take a shine to Katniss, though, identifying with her stubborn nature and unwillingness to listen to figures of authority, and before long, the two are essentially working together to try and protect the genuinely kind and good-hearted Peeta.

When Katniss and Peeta are allowed to jointly win the 74th Games, Snow wants revenge after a teenage girl makes him look like a fool. As a result, the Third Quarter Quell, the 75th Games, only pulls existing victors back into the arena ... and Peeta volunteers when Haymitch's name is called, sending him and Katniss back into the arena just a year after their win. These Games end abruptly, however, when Katniss fires an arrow through the force field surrounding the arena. She and Haymitch then decamp to the rebellious District 13, while Peeta is captured.

Sources indicate that eventually, the rebellion succeeds, Snow is defeated, and Katniss, Peeta, and Haymitch live out the rest of their lives in District 12. Hence, "Sunrise on the Reaping" fits perfectly into the existing "Hunger Games" movie timeline (it marries "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and the stories that kicked off the Hunger Games franchise), and it's in theaters starting tonight.

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Recent findings suggest that google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

In a recent development, to me, this is the most useful fresh feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each proposal includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is presently open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

It has been revealed that plans can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

In a recent development, pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

If you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

Recent findings suggest that these updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand.

Patch: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix states that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build latest production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”.

Industry observers note that apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report states “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”.

Apple stated back in June that the company was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

Yellowjackets Season 4 Review: The Survival Thriller's Final Episodes Answer A Major Question

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, "What are we capable of when our darkest urges are given not only a voice, but also a stage on which to use it?
  • Set in both the late 1990s and early 2020s, "Yellowjackets" follows the aftermath of a plane crash that was taking the Wiskayok, Upcoming Jersey Yellowjackets soccer team across the country to a national championship.
  • "Yellowjackets" returns from a third season that hit some stumbling blocks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, "What are we capable of when our darkest urges are given not only a voice, but also a stage on which to use it? And can you ever really go back once you've seen what's underneath?" asked Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson in the pitch deck for their thriller series "Yellowjackets," claiming this would be the central question driving their show. As "Yellowjackets" debuts its fourth and final season, its answer comes due.

Set in both the late 1990s and early 2020s, "Yellowjackets" follows the aftermath of a plane crash that was taking the Wiskayok, Upcoming Jersey Yellowjackets soccer team across the country to a national championship. The teenage survivors descend into a barbarity, cannibalism, and pagan ritual across 19 months stranded in the Canadian wilderness. In their present, their now middle-aged selves reckon with old wounds coming unsealed.

"Yellowjackets" returns from a third season that hit some stumbling blocks. The departure of Juliette Lewis in particular was a hard void to fill, even if the show is trying with the introduction of Hilary Swank as an adult counterpart to Yellowjacket Melissa (Jenna Burgess). But the season ended on a high note.

It has been revealed that in the Season 3 finale, "Full Circle," Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) uses a salvaged satellite phone to call for rescue. With help's imminent arrival in the Wilderness, the Yellowjackets must scramble to tie up loose ends. In the present, Taissa (Tawny Cypress) and Misty (Christina Ricci), fed up with cleaning Shauna's (Melanie Lynskey) messes, are planning to kill her — until Melissa puts the spotlight on the Yellowjackets again.

Paramount+ has only shared the first two (out of ten) episodes of "Yellowjackets" Season 4 for review. Going off that extremely limited view of the season, the ride is steady enough so far.

It's been a nail-biting wait for the return of "Yellowjackets," especially knowing since last October this would be the end of the show. I'll admit I've been counting down the weeks for Season 4, yet when I first received those screeners, I held off for several days. Suddenly the reality of the show ending, and the risk of it disappointing, became too real.

As previously confirmed by the creators, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 is the most structurally complex season yet. Now there are three parallel timelines, as we see play out in these first two episodes. The adult Yellowjackets are still in one story, but the teens are in two. Instead of depicting their rescue and readjustment in chronological order, Season 4 cuts back and forth between their last days in the wilderness and their first days back in Wiskoyak. Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown) is taking lead as the one keeping the other Yellowjackets on script — she does grow up to be a lawyer and politician, after all.

In a recent development, knowing "Yellowjackets" was originally planned for five seasons, it's tempting to consider if this latest structure is a way to cram the remainder of the 1990s timeline into one densely-packed season. Indeed, we see very little of the Wilderness timeline in these first two episodes, which will frustrate some since that's still the most exciting storyline. It's got the running clock, as the Yellowjackets have to get their stories and evidence straight without knowing exactly when help is arriving, and the biggest mysteries, since we know that a few more of the Yellowjackets are going to die in the time gap.

It has been revealed that "Yellowjackets" Season 3 previously skipped months ahead of Season 2's cliffhanger ending. Watching the Season 4 premiere, with the Yellowjackets recuperating in a hospital, you might think the show has done so again. After all, Season 3 ended with Nat calling for help, so it's not a huge jump. Plus, is there any more story to tell in the Wilderness? Indeed there is, because the last minutes cut back and forth to violence still unseen. But is it wise to fall back on the "keep the audience waiting" trick in your last season?

Opening on the immediate post-rescue timeline, though, delivers on a promise the show has made since the beginning. Since we've known from the jump that some of the team makes it home, the show invites you to imagine what will happen when that moment arrives. How will they adjust to seeing their old parents and peers again, who have no idea what their daughters and friends faced for 19 months? The Season 4 premiere finally introduces many of the characters' parents, and sets up a season exploring the Yellowjackets' home lives, like what made them into the people they were before the Wilderness.

How does the 1990s timeline bridge to the 2020s one? How do the Yellowjackets assimilate to suburban mundanity? How will they handle the unwanted public spotlight that flattens them into sainted heroes but also piles on the salacious theories of what they did to survive? How do they cover up any and all investigations into their crimes that still remain buried as of 2022? "Yellowjackets" Season 4 is on track to deliver all those answers and, so far, they appear promising.

As for the 2020s timeline, the premiere picks up with Melissa, catching up to where she went after running off in Season 3 Episode 9 "How The Story Ends." The show still hasn't quite overcome what a narrative patch her introduction was back in Season 3. Now, though, she is at least giving the present day timeline a villain and conflict uniting the other Yellowjackets, something the show has struggled with after Season 1.

In a recent development, the adult timeline of "Yellowjackets" is often best when the leads are together. In Season 4, they're sharing a united front early on instead of converging mid-season. Let's also just say that how Melissa re-inserts herself into her old friends' lives fits the absurdist black comedy the show excels at, and it's looking like it could be an impetus for the Yellowjackets to finally earn a public reckoning.

Conversely, the teen timeline looks like it might be splitting the girls up as they slot back into their old, separate lives without the Wilderness binding them together. But the teen timeline actors, who've always held the show up through peaks and valleys, remain as strong as ever.

Shauna's (Sophie Nélisse) brief reign as the Wilderness' cannibal Antler Queen is over, and she's not happy about it. She says very little as her anger stews; she's cowed and quiet, but not regretful. Episode 2 focuses mostly on Shauna, and the very beginning of how she's going to force herself into a box of domestic tranquility for two decades — a box that her middle-aged self is breaking out of. Shauna's mask is off again and it's scary, and also incredible how Melanie Lynskey makes her sweet, high-pitched voice sound as cold and sharp as an icicle.

The show's usual MVPs remain Sophie Thatcher in the teen timeline — Natalie is the one Yellowjacket not returning to a happy home — and Christina Ricci in the adult timeline. Misty's manically planning to stage Shauna's suicide brings out her unhinged comic relief side; no one can do a wide-eyed, violent smile like Ricci.

Yet, dialogue is a mixed bag. There's plenty of clever and cutting lines, but a bit too much hand-holding exposition recaps, as well. The killer soundtrack of "Yellowjackets," though, remains on point, bringing out '90s favorites like Nirvana and Depeche Mode for montage sequences. The most striking needle drop is in Episode 2, when Shauna is walking alone at night (a genuinely eerie shot) to Portishead's "Wandering Star.".

In a recent development, blunt yet clever visual storytelling is on the menu in these episodes, too. Take Lottie (Courtney Eaton) sitting in a hospital exam room where the wall is painted with a forest full of Disney-like animals, a reminder of her abandoned Wilderness home. Continuing on from a dream sequence in Season 3 Episode 8's "A Normal Boring Life," Season 4 Episode 2 uses a grocery store as the ultimate setting of modern normality (the contrast, of course, is that the Yellowjackets had to fight and scavenge for their food in the Wilderness).

Recent findings suggest that shauna is surrounded by seemingly innocuous reminders of her last 19 months as the group's butcher (in more ways than one), like sliced deli meat or a dead deer (crowned with antlers) being sliced up as roadkill. If this season can stick the landing, the legacy of "Yellowjackets" should be stronger than Shauna's as the Antler Queen.

"Yellowjackets" Season 4 premieres on Paramount+ on Friday, November 20, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, director Brian Duffield is a cinephile who watches a lot of movies, but when the time came to direct his adventure film “Whalefall” he was dismayed to realize he couldn’t think of a single film he could look to as a model. “It was a nightmare for that reason,” Duffield told IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “It also the joy of it, having a room full of amazingly gifted artists all starting from this place of real befuddlement.”.

It has been revealed that in the movie, Austin Abrams plays a scuba diver who gets swallowed by a sperm whale and has only an hour of oxygen to keep him alive while he tries to escape; it’s a premise that posed multiple challenges for Duffield and his team, starting with the question of how exactly to build the stomach that Abrams would be trapped inside for the majority of the film — and how to shoot those scenes. Related Stories Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media Hires Former Netflix Exec Tendo Nagenda as President Fall Festival Movies Sold: Magnolia Heaps Dollars on ‘Trash Mountain’ with Caleb Hearon and Zooey Deschanel.

Recent findings suggest that “It wasn’t normal coverage,” Duffield mentioned. “Even a shot of Austin just sitting in the stomach required months of preparation and planning — every shot of him in the stomach is, by its nature, a stunt.” The ultimate effect onscreen is terrifying, but on set Duffield states the stomach scenes looked more than a little ridiculous. “The set looked crazy. From the outside it’s this black weird bag, and then it’s on a gimbal so it’s moving, and it’s full of water.”.

According to recent reports, to give the impression of the stomach chewing, Duffield’s crew found an old-school, practical solution. “When the stomach chews, it compresses,” Duffield said. “The way we did that is we just had burly men jump onto it. Austin’s inside, and there’s a guy with a camera, and I can’t fit in the stomach so I’m just watching these Fresh Zealanders leap and compress, then I’m hearing Austin scream.” Although Duffield planned his shots meticulously, he often found that the stomach had a mind of its own and required swift adaptation from the crew.

According to recent reports, “There’s water in the stomach, and we would drain it every night,” Duffield mentioned. “The material that the stomach was made of would change shape overnight, and we’d come back to resume a scene, and our set would be a different set — we’d fill it with water, and it would all lay different.” Doors also contracted due to humidity and other conditions. “By the end of the shoot, there were so many jagged doors that we’d cut for cameras.”.

Ultimately, all of Duffield’s storyboards “went out the window” because the stomach kept changing shape, and Abrams couldn’t roll in the planned directions. “The stomach was kind of directing the movie,” Duffield noted. “Austin and I had to sync up and figure out how, with this fresh environment every day, to get the shots that tell the story as cleanly as possible.” That was no easy task, especially since the set’s very nature made it hard to acclimate the audience geographically.

“It sounds ridiculous, but we had so many conversations about trying to get an audience to see that ‘that sphincter leads to the throat,’ or ‘that sphincter leads to the second stomach,'” Duffield said, adding that he constantly had to think about how one shot would connect to another to let the audience know where Abrams was inside the whale. “Austin’s moving around the whole time, and the stomach goes in every direction. Bit by bit, shot by shot, every shot is its own unique challenge.”.

Visual effects supervisor Guillaume Rocheron worked with Duffield and the camera team to come up with visual cues that could help the audience follow Abrams’ journey through the whale, but the task was further complicated by the fact that the audience was sharing his point of view — and for long portions of the story, Abrams’ character was supposed to be confused. “Austin’s character doesn’t have a lot of information about what is happening to him,” Duffield remarked. “You want the audience to have the same information as him, but not get so lost and confused that they’re out of the movie.”.

It has been revealed that duffield knew that striking that balance would be tricky throughout production and editing. “It’s hard to have a character in a situation he doesn’t know anything about and then have an audience get invested,” Duffield noted, adding that the usual test screening questions were useless here. “It’s the classic test screening thing: ‘Is there anything that’s confusing to you?'” Luckily, Duffield worked with master editor Pietro Scalia, who worked with the director to find the most straightforward way to connect the audience to the material.

“We eventually concluded, just focus on Austin,” Duffield stated. “Austin is dynamite, and he’s carrying you, and the more you’re in lockstep with Austin, you’re going to be okay.” The key, Duffield felt, was to preserve the illusion of reality at every possible moment. “ When we were editing and sound designing, it was just like, ‘How do we keep trying to make it feel real?’ I’m a very pro-CG guy, but even if there’s some stitching from a stuntman or a digital double to Austin, Austin’s in every shot of the scene. I think some of the things that people think is a digital double are not a digital double — it’s Austin just getting yanked around and fighting for his life.”.

Though Duffield is sure Abrams wouldn’t want to return for a sequel, he stated his lead actor was as up for the physical demands of the role as the department heads were for the mental and logistical challenges — challenges unlike any they had ever faced. “Nothing any of us had done before applied to this project,” Duffield said, adding that nothing they learned would apply to future projects given the singular nature of “Whalefall.” “It was really challenging, but I was looking for that kind of filmmaking challenge. It was the hardest shoot I’ll probably ever have, but everyone was also giddy about it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's quickly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

Sources indicate that this earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Sources indicate that bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her newly introduced direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she notes more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

She'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time Fresh York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that the significant life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

Mind you, the movie comes out on Wednesday to get in on the holiday, meaning it will have a full five-day Wednesday to Sunday stretch. So, that $56 million figure isn't a standard weekend figure. Meanwhile, the holiday's other major release, the Hailee Steinfeld-led Disney animated flick "Hexed," is targeting a softer opening in the $30 million range.

In a recent development, if all goes well for Universal Pictures, then, "Focker-In-Law" may take the number one spot ... that is, unless Lionsgate has anything to say about it. Indeed, the studio's "Hunger Games" film "Sunrise on the Reaping" is shaping up to be a massive hit, pulling in at least $100 million domestically this upcoming weekend. As such, assuming it's not too front-loaded, it could compete with the Focker family for the crown during its second frame.

Industry observers note that ben Stiller's "Meet the Parents" buried Sylvester Stallone's "Get Carter" at the box office back in 2000, eventually pulling in $330 million worldwide on a $55 million budget. "Meet the Fockers" was an even bigger success, earning over $500 million on an $80 million budget. The problem? By the time "Little Fockers" came along in 2010, the franchise was running out of gas. Against a $100 million budget, it made $310 million.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, $310 million is nothing to sneeze at. Nevertheless, "Focker-In-Law," has to pay stars Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Blythe Danner, Owen Wilson, Ariana Grande, and (to a lesser degree) Skyler Gisondo, meaning it's likely its budget is once again in the $100 million range.

According to recent reports, even so, with an over/under $50 million debut over a typically robust holiday weekend, that's a damn good start. "Moana 2" smashed box office records leading to the biggest Thanksgiving ever in 2024, for example. This year won't be as significant, but families go to the movies around the holidays. And when we consider that this franchise has generally performed well overseas, international audiences should turn up as well. (Notably, Paramount is handling overseas distribution.).

Comedy could use a win, too. Earlier this year, two very different comedies in "One Night Only" and "Super Troopers 3" both flopped at the box office on the same weekend. As such, the only true, blue comedy success story of 2026 is "Scary Movie" ($231 million worldwide). Fittingly, that was another revival of an early 2000s-born franchise that's long been dormant. The difference is that we're talking about something more family-friendly with "Fock-In-Law," so that helps.

Moreover, most recent comedy hits have been rom-coms like "Ticket to Paradise" ($168 million), "The Lost City" ($192 million), and "Anyone But You" ($220 million). "Focker-In-Law," by comparison, is much more comedy-forward. However, it does have a central romantic element, which should only further aid its cause.

Recent findings suggest that basically, this one has a good shot at attracting audiences eager to catch up with characters they haven't seen in a while, with or without critics on its side. We'll see how everything pans out.

There are also questions about the GTA 6 autosave function and how it works, which we can also help explain.

Here's the lowdown on exactly how to save in GTA 6 and how the game's autosave works — and why it might seem like it isn't working at all.

To manually save in GTA 6, you need to pause the game, navigate to the "Game" option on the menu, then select "Save." This will show 15 save slots, of which you can choose any to save your game. If you suspect you may want to load an old save to play through missions another way or make a different choice, I'd recommend using a rolling save system, where every time you save, you overwrite the oldest save file you have.

It has been revealed that however, there are restrictions around when you can manually save. You cannot save during a mission, if you're in combat, if you have a wanted level, or if you're falling. Therefore, you must wait until a moment of calm to save your game.

GTA 6 does have an autosave function, however it's a little sporadic in how it actually works. The game should autosave after missions are completed, whether they are main missions or optional ones. However, there are reports that this hasn't been working properly, so you should be manually saving your game on a regular basis in case the autosave lets you down.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

According to recent reports, that's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a fresh "View Once" option as well.

Sources indicate that as WABetaInfo highlights, the first time you use this feature, WhatsApp will present a pop-up explaining the feature, how "View Once text gives you more privacy," and that when you send the message, it'll disappear from the chat after the recipient opens it. WhatsApp also explains that recipients cannot share, forward, save, or take screenshots of View Once text messages. Recipients won't see the text appear in the usual chat interface, either; instead, your recipient will need to open the message in a separate window. Once they close this page, the message disappears.

According to recent reports, as mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That said, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.).

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest enhancement. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

"I am in here." Set in a bizarre near-future society where corporations sponsor calendar years, the plot (such as it is) follows several interconnected characters and institutions, particularly a prestigious tennis academy and a nearby addiction recovery facility.

Meanwhile, a mysterious film known as Infinite Jest possesses such extraordinary entertainment value that viewers become incapable of doing anything except watching it (a prescient metaphor for the attention-consuming devices we all now carry around in our pockets). "Caddy smelled like trees." William Faulkner has written several books that continue to be discussed and taught in literature courses around the globe, though perhaps the most well-regarded of them is The Sound and the Fury. It's a modernist landmark, chronicling the decline of the once-prominent Compson family in the South. The book is divided into four sections, each presenting a different perspective on the family's troubled history.

Industry observers note that the first is narrated by Benjy Compson, a man with an intellectual disability, and the writing immerses us inside his fragmented perception of time. Subsequent sections explore the psychological struggles of his brothers Quentin and Jason, before the final portion zeroes in on the Compsons' Black housekeeper. "Call me Ishmael." Here, we meet Ishmael, a sailor who joins the crew of the whaling ship Pequod, commanded by the formidable Captain Ahab. However, Ahab has little interest in conducting an ordinary whaling expedition. Instead, he's consumed by an obsessive desire to kill Moby Dick, an enormous white sperm whale responsible for taking his leg during an earlier encounter. As the Pequod ventures across the oceans, Ahab's increasingly destructive obsession threatens to doom everyone aboard.

It has been revealed that although the main storyline may seem relatively straightforward, Moby-Dick is really a much more complicated, layered work. These digressions can occasionally test readers' patience, but they're essential to the overall effect. Once again, this is a book that wasn't fully embraced on release, but nowadays, many consider Moby-Dick to be the Great American Novel.

In a recent development, indeed, the influence of One Hundred Years of Solitude is immense, with countless writers drawing inspiration from it. Authors such as Salman Rushdie, Toni Morrison, and Carlos Fuentes have all praised it, while Chilean poet Pablo Neruda famously called it "the greatest revelation in the Spanish language since Don Quixote." The book won a bevy of awards when it came out, and contributed to the author receiving the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature.

A vivid time capsule of the Roaring Twenties, as well as a timeless statement on the promises and disappointments of the American Dream. The tale is told by Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman who becomes fascinated by his mysterious, fabulously wealthy neighbor, Jay Gatsby. Behind Gatsby's carefully cultivated persona lies an obsessive desire to reunite with Daisy Buchanan, a married woman he loved years earlier.

According to recent reports, what might have been a glamorous romance instead develops into a devastating examination of wealth, class, ambition, and the impossibility of reclaiming the past. There is so much wisdom and bittersweet emotion here, despite the book's relatively modest length of 180 pages. When The Great Gatsby was first published, peers like T.S. Elliot and Gertrude Stein praised it. Today, it appears on countless 'greatest novels' lists and is taught in high schools all over the world.

"There is no greatness where there is not simplicity, goodness, and truth." This one is so highly regarded worldwide that its title is sometimes used as a shorthand for literary excellence. Set against the Napoleonic Wars, War and Peace follows several aristocratic Russian families as they become entangled with some of the most consequential events in European history. The cast includes the idealistic Pierre Bezukhov, the disillusioned Prince Andrei Bolkonsky, and the spirited Natasha Rostova.

Each of these characters undergoes a profound personal transformation over the course of the book. Through their experiences, Tolstoy explores everything from love and mortality to the nature of history and the forces that shape human destiny. It's remarkable that he's able to nimbly combine all these elements. Indeed, his prose moves effortlessly between lavish aristocratic gatherings, devastating battlefield scenes, and quiet moments of introspection, making for a detailed portrait of Russian society.

"History, Stephen remarked, is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake." Many regard this cryptic, boundary-pushing book to be the greatest English-language novel of the 20th century. Taking place over a single day in Dublin, June 16, 1904, Ulysses centers on three characters: Leopold Bloom, an advertising salesman; Stephen Dedalus, a young intellectual; and Molly Bloom, Leopold's wife. Their seemingly ordinary experiences form the foundation of an extraordinarily ambitious literary experiment, loosely modeled on Homer's 'Odyssey'.

Rather than depicting heroic adventures, writer James Joyce transforms everyday encounters, mundane activities, and private thoughts into an epic exploration of human consciousness. The prose itself conveys this. The author employs a dizzying assortment of narrative techniques, including stream of consciousness, elaborate wordplay, parody, and radical stylistic experimentation. Not for nothing, many literary heavyweights have declared Ulysses to be a masterpiece, including Faulkner, Hemingway, and T.S. Eliot.

Not only does this mark the best preview gross for a Hunger Games movie since the second installment, 2013's Catching Fire ($25.2 million), it sees the movie beating the $17.6 million previews of Christopher Nolan's record-breaking epic The Odyssey. At the time, The Odyssey had the best preview grosses of the year. So far, it has only been surpassed by Spider-Man: Brand Latest Day ($72 million) and Sunrise, giving the latter the second-biggest previews of 2026 year-to-date.

There is at least one remaining 2026 movie that is expected to have bigger previews than Sunrise on the Reaping, namely the Marvel Cinematic Universe's Spider-Man: Brand New Day follow-up Avengers: Doomsday. However, other strong contenders include Dune: Part Three and Jumanji: Open World. Regardless, Sunrise on the Reaping's performance is remarkable. Below, see how it compares to the previous Hunger Games movies:.

The Hunger Games: Catching Fire (2013).

The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 1 (2014).

The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2 (2015).

The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023).

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (2026).

Industry observers note that it is worth noting that, while this chart is not adjusted for inflation, every installment in the franchise except the original has debuted in the same pre-Thanksgiving frame, making them especially comparable. Not only has Sunrise on the Reaping reversed the downward trend that the franchise has been experiencing since 2014, it has brought it back up to nearly the same level as Catching Fire, which remains the highest-grossing installment.

While preview numbers are not always a reliable predictor of a movie's ultimate performance, if the upcoming installment has a similar trajectory to Catching Fire (which it could - Sunrise on the Reaping reviews have earned it a Verified Hot audience score of 95% on Rotten Tomatoes, improving upon Catching Fire's 89% and marking the best of the franchise), it could ultimately open to $133.3 million (the third-best debut of the franchise) and gross $733.5 million worldwide (the third-best overall haul as well).

Critics have given Sunrise on the Reaping 68% on the Rotten Tomatoes Tomatometer, which is the fifth-best for the franchise ahead of Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

Should The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping climb that high by the end of its run (against a reported budget of roughly $200 million), it will reestablish the franchise as a major player in the box office arena. In fact, if it does debut above $100 million, it will be the first Lionsgate movie to do so since Mockingjay – Part 2 11 years ago (though they got close with the smash hit Michael Jackson biopic Michael, which earned a 3-day debut of $97.2 million).
