In 2025, "Hunger Games" author Suzanne Collins released one of the most long-awaited stories in the entire franchise — the backstory of District 12 victor Haymitch Abernathy, "Sunrise on the Reaping." A film adaptation titled "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" immediately took shape, and after Joseph Zada was cast as a young version of Haymitch — before he's an aging, depressed, drink-swilling lout portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the four original films — the rest of the cast began to round out.

According to recent reports, immediately after I read the book, I wondered who might be cast as Lenore Dove Baird, the beautiful and wild girlfriend Haymitch is forced to leave behind in District 12 when he's essentially chosen to participate in the Games by mistake. I was then extremely pleased when Whitney Peak was cast in this vital part, who's not only Haymitch's love interest but a vital link to the other prequel "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" ... in that Lenore Dove is distantly related to that film and novel's heroine Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler).

So where have you seen Peak before she took on the role of Lenore Dove? I should say that, in general, Peak's star is still on the rise, but there's a reason she earned this role; not only is she extremely talented, but she's appeared in some pretty high-profile projects in recent years. From a major HBO reboot (that did fail, by no fault of Peak's) to some independent films, here's where you've seen Whitney Peak, who plays Lenore Dove in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," before.

After small roles in films like "Molly's Game" and TV reveals like "The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina," Whitney Peak booked her first lead role courtesy of the "Gossip Girl" reboot that aired on HBO Max from 2021 to 2023.

According to recent reports, as a huge fan of the ridiculous campfest that is the original "Gossip Girl" — which was adapted, very loosely, from a novel series written by Cecily von Ziegesar and ran on The CW from 2007 to 2012 — I was excited for this reboot, but sadly, it was a largely toothless and lackluster impersonation of the original. Still, Peak was very good! She plays Zoya Lott, a newcomer to the high-status New York City preparatory school who finds out that her late birth mother had another daughter. After Zoya and her half-sister, the wealthy and popular Julien Calloway (Jordan Alexander), make intends to meet up, they end up attending Constance Billard together ... but Zoya, who doesn't come from extreme privilege, struggles to fit in with Julien and her high society friends.

Sources indicate that again, this version of "Gossip Girl" is entirely too concerned with social justice crusades, whereas in the original show, the 20-somethings did insane stuff like sell each other for hotels. (Social justice is ... just not the point of a show like "Gossip Girl!") It was ultimately canceled after its Season 2 finale aired, leaving the story unfinished ... but it also freed Peak up for bigger and better opportunities.

In terms of her massive-screen work, Whitney Peak has appeared in a solid mix of independent project and a few bigger movies — aside from "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." In 2022, Peak showed up in the supporting role of Becca in the legacy sequel "Hocus Pocus 2," and I already mentioned that she was in "Molly's Game," which marked her film debut.

It has been revealed that elsewhere, Peak led films like the independent horror movie "Eye for an Eye," directed by Colin Tilley and adapted from Elisa Victoria's book "Mr. Sandman" — in that, Peak plays a young woman grieving the tragic loss of her parents who finds herself newly traumatized by a shocking, violent incident in her new home in Florida. Peak also appeared in the action thriller "Trap House" alongside Sophia Lillis, Inde Navarrette, Jack Champion, and Bobby Cannavale, as well as Tommy Wirkola's survival film "Thrash" with Phoebe Dynevor and Djimon Hounsou.

You can see Peak as Lenore Dove Baird in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" in theaters now.

The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Review: Fincher And Tarantino's Mean-Spirited Hollywood Sequel

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there was a time in my life when a movie made by David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino would be the biggest cinematic event ever.
  • As for Tarantino, while he tends to make everyone's eyes roll when he gives a fresh hot take-laden interview, I still think he has the juice.
  • Industry observers note that but his previous film, "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," might just be his best.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there was a time in my life when a movie made by David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino would be the biggest cinematic event ever. Not to get all film bro on you, but Fincher and Tarantino were very important filmmakers to me in my youth. That's not to say they aren't still important to me now ... but the luster has faded a bit. Fincher has spent the last few years making movies specifically for Netflix, and while those films — "Mank" and "The Killer" — have their charms, they pale in comparison to his previous work, so much so that I'd say the last great movie was "Gone Girl" in 2014 (for what it's worth, Fincher's exclusivity with Netflix is now over).

As for Tarantino, while he tends to make everyone's eyes roll when he gives a fresh hot take-laden interview, I still think he has the juice. However, the "Pulp Fiction" auteur has decided that he will only direct 10 movies and then hang up his filmmaking spurs. Because of this, Tarantino seems hesitant to direct a movie again, since that hypothetical movie would be his last. He came close to making "The Movie Critic" only to drop the idea entirely, and now he's working on directing his first stage play, "The Popinjay Cavalier.".

Industry observers note that but his previous film, "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," might just be his best. It's certainly near and dear to my heart, as I find it inherently rewatchable. It's a funny, sad, surprisingly sweet hang-out movie that doubles as a slice of alternate Hollywood history. Tarantino has now returned to the world of "Hollywood" with his upcoming script, but again, since he doesn't want to direct his tenth and final movie just yet, he's handed the project over to Fincher.

All of this is a long-winded way of saying that everything about "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" should, in theory, appeal to me, a movie nerd who still considers Fincher and Tarantino to be among the greats. But Fincher's not-so-stellar Netflix output coupled with Tarantino's weird insistence on not directing the movie himself muted my enthusiasm a bit, as have some lackluster trailers. On top of all that, Fincher and Tarantino have vastly different movie making styles. Would a union between the pair even work? I'm pleased to say the answer is "Yes." Sort of. While I was cautious about "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," it eventually won me over. But it's not quite the movie I think anyone is expecting, and that's going to catch a few folks off guard.

"Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" introduced us to washed-up actor Rick Dalton, played by Leonardo DiCaprio, and his trusty stunt man sidekick Cliff Booth, played by Brad Pitt. Pitt turned in a funny, scene-stealing performance that landed him an Oscar, but Cliff seemed destined to be a supporting player in Rick's life. "Cliff Booth" turns him into a leading man, and I'm not entirely sure that's a good idea. Because without Rick Dalton by his side, what is Cliff Booth? I think the case can be made that Cliff Booth is a very charming psychopath. He's certainly not against brutally murdering people, and while he's highly capable and smooth as silk, there doesn't seem to be a whole lot going on in Cliff Booth's head. Rick and his internal struggles were part of what gave "Hollywood" its heart. Without him around, "Cliff Booth" ends up frequently feeling cold and cruel.

According to recent reports, pitt's Cliff became so lovable and likable in the first movie that I can't help but think Tarantino, always one to subvert expectations, is deliberately hammering home the point that for all his charms, Cliff is not exactly a good guy. He's a cypher; an idealized version of machismo — a men's pulp magazine hero brought to life. He lives fast and hard, likes drugs and booze, constantly risks life and limb, flirts with every woman he encounters, can kick everyone's butt, and still finds time to chill out and watch TV with his dear old dad. And yes, he occasionally murders people. Is "Cliff Booth" an attempt by Tarantino, or maybe Fincher, to remind us that this guy isn't nearly as cool as he seems?

In "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," it's 1977, and Cliff's movie stunt days seem to behind him, especially since Rick Dalton has moved to Australia, where he's at the moment starring on a popular Aussie TV show. Cliff keeps busy, though, working an assortment of odd jobs. He runs the projector at the New Beverly Cinema, he works as a bartender making all sorts of elaborate margaritas, he participates in a demolition derby, and he even occasionally appears in an X-rated movie or two.

Recent findings suggest that on the side, however, Cliff also works as a fixer for some of his old Hollywood friends. If they get into a jam that they can't go to the cops about, Cliff is willing to step in and work something out — for a price. And sometimes that results in a body count.

Cliff has become a legend due to his fight with Bruce Lee and the time he killed those damn hippies who broke into Rick's home (it's also worth noting that in "Hollywood," people suspected Cliff of murdering his wife, although that incident isn't mentioned here). At the end of the day, Cliff comes home to the apartment he shares with his dad Gus (Peter Weller) to watch old movies and TV. Weller's Gus is the warmest part of this surprisingly cold movie, and the banter between Cliff and his father is laid-back and believable in a way that made me wish the entire movie was just the two of them shooting the breeze.

"Cliff Booth" is in no hurry, but eventually a shaggy Hollywood crime thriller plot emerges. The logistics of what's going on are hilariously convoluted, but Cliff is hired by manic actor Charlie Peters (Scott Caan, looking eerily like his late father in nearly every frame) to help get him out of some trouble. Cliff doesn't exactly like Charlie, but he does like Charlie's wife Toni (Carla Gugino), whom he had a love affair with over a decade ago. And Cliff really likes Charlie's agent, amazonian goddess Karen Crosby, played Elizabeth Debicki.

The flirty relationship between Cliff and Karen is meant to be sweet and romantic, but while Pitt and Debicki are both quite good in their respective roles (Debicki is particularly funny, bugging her eyes out at all the ludicrous things that happen), they don't have much chemistry. There's the glimmer of something interesting in how Cliff reveals he's a masochist who gets off on the idea of Karen slapping him around, but this angle is ultimately treated as little more than a throwaway gag.

According to recent reports, while "Cliff Booth" has the same hang-out movie vibes as "Hollywood," there are bursts of brutal violence that left me uncomfortable. Tarantino is no stranger to violence, and the major finale of "Hollywood" is drenched in blood. But here is where the styles of Fincher and Tarantino seem to clash the most. Tarantino's violence is almost always hyper-stylized and over-the-top. Influenced by countless splatter flicks and kung-fu movies, Tarantino shoots his violence in ways that are so ludicrously graphic that they become funny in a twisted sort of way.

It has been revealed that fincher, however, has a more realistic approach, which results in a handful of brutal scenes — most notably when the film's villains, a pair of gangsters from the Philippines (played by Matt Groove and JB Tadena) butcher an entire family during a home invasion. This moment has no bearing on Cliff's story, and seems to only exist to show us how bad these bad guys are. Which is fine, in theory, but Fincher stages it in such a cruel, unpleasant way that when he tries to lighten the mood in the following scenes, it rings hollow.

Industry observers note that there's a conversation worth having here about movie violence, I suppose. Which is the more questionable approach: depicting these moments in an unrealistic over-the-top fashion, or making them as real (and therefore upsetting) as possible? Again, I can't help but think that Tarantino is intentionally trying to flip the script and deliver something harsher after the good vibes of "Hollywood." The '60s are over, and here we're at the tail-end of the '70s, nearing the '80s. It makes sense for the vibes to be drastically different. But intentional or not, this contrast between Fincher and Tarantino makes "Cliff Booth" more mean-spirited than expected.

Midway through the film, Tarantino's script gives Karen a meaty monologue about movies. Before becoming an agent, Karen was a budding film critic, and in her professional opinion, movies should entertain above all else. While she thinks movies can be artistic, she doesn't think of them as art. It's 1977, and the movie everyone is talking about is "Star Wars," which Karen thinks proves her point: audiences don't want a fancy cinematic meal, they want movie fast food. Even "The Godfather" is little more than pulp in her estimation.

It has been revealed that I don't think a lifelong movie nerd like Tarantino actually believes this (and I don't think Fincher does, either), but this little speech must be here for a reason. Are we meant to just sit back and enjoy the ride of "Cliff Booth" and not think too much about what's unfolding here? Or is the film itself trying to prove Karen's theory wrong? For all it's moments of comedy, there's a cold darkness lurking beneath "Cliff Booth" that keeps it from being fully entertaining. It's as if Fincher and Tarantino don't quite have a grasp on the material.

It has been revealed that regardless, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is Fincher's best movie in years — since "Gone Girl," really. While I do think he and Tarantino don't quite mix as well as we'd all hoped, the material has energized the filmmaker to craft a great-looking movie with several standout set pieces (I particularly liked a montage, told entirely via press photographs, showing Karen attending the premiere of "Looking for Mr. Goodbar").

Still, I can't help but wish Tarantino had just gone ahead and directed this himself. If he had, I think the tonal clashes might've been smoothed out considerably. "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" felt like something of a masterpiece to me when I first saw it, and the film's hefty runtime was a blessing rather than a curse — I wanted to spend as much time in this world with these characters as possible.

But that world is nowhere to be found in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." Tarantino clearly didn't want to tread the same ground all over again when he banged out this script, and there's nothing wrong with that. But if everything is so different this time around, why would we want to check back in with Cliff at all, then? Especially without Rick by his side? "Cliff Booth" builds towards a memorable, brutal, action-packed climax before just sort of giving up and rolling credits. It's as if, in the end, everyone involved realized that old "Hollywood" magic was finally gone.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" will be released exclusively in IMAX on November 25, 2026 for a two-week engagement before streaming on Netflix December 23, 2026.

#4681. Breaking: I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

Breaking: I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better?
  • Sources indicate that you'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up.
  • Proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better? Pangram is one of the leaders in the field, promising a "near-zero false positive rate" by looking at "subtle cues" in the writing, based on a training and feedback model comparing human-made content with the AI equivalent.

Sources indicate that you'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up. After a short story was flagged by Pangram and then judged to be free from AI, the detection engine has been accused of bias against text from minority writers.

Proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written. So far, the reward is unclaimed.

Sources indicate that as the AI detector has recently added AI image and video detection to its capabilities, it seemed a good time to put Pangram's analysis skills to the test for myself. Here's how it performed in the three different content types.

On the human side, I picked out 10 of my most recent articles for Lifehacker, known to be written by a person because I personally wrote them—in the traditional way, I fretted over word choices, went back and changed sentences, and accidentally left in a variety of typos that editors thankfully fixed.

For the AI content, I rotated between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, and got the LLMs to write 10 articles with the same headlines and the same approximate number of words, for a tech-savvy audience. I even asked the AI apps to vary their language use, so that the output would "read less like an LLM has written it.".

Pangram's AI text detector lets you upload files, but to make the task a little harder, I copied and pasted all of the text into the online article, so it wouldn't be able to rely on any metadata included in the file. The scans got the correct result each and every time: Human-written text came back as 100% human, and AI-written text came back as 100% AI.

In a recent development, what's more, Pangram was certain about its results. All of the human writing was marked as highly likely to be human, and the vast majority of the AI writing was marked as highly likely to have come from an LLM. There were only a handful of phrases or sentences across thousands of AI words that got a "medium" rather than a "high" ranking for AI.

In a recent development, now, there have been some edge cases where Pangram has got it wrong—like a poem repeating the same six words thousands of times—but as far as this sample goes, it can't be faulted. Clearly, my writing is too idiosyncratic and too clunky to be confused for the smooth sheen of AI-produced prose.

To be fair, I do have another advantage over AI: I can actually test out devices and apps in a way that LLM bots can't. ChatGPT can't experiment with One UI 9 (at least not yet), though it can scrape the web for various experiments and tests that real people have done.

Sources indicate that however, I was able to fool Pangram to some extent by alternating AI paragraphs with human-written paragraphs. The text was flagged as AI, but the percentage estimate was typically lower (20-25%) than what it actually was (around 50%). If you're offloading some but not all of your writing to AI, some of it might slip though as real.

According to recent reports, image and video detection is the new string to Pangram's bow, so I sifted through my phone's photo and video library for some pieces of content to test the AI on. Again, I used copy and paste to get the files into Pangram rather than uploading them, to limit how much information the AI detector could get from metadata.

It has been revealed that again, all the human-made content was recognized as such, with a very high level of certainty—whether it was complicated crowd shots or simpler images of natural scenes. Presumably, there are even more signals to go off than there are with writing, including camera movements, colors, style, consistency, and composition.

In a recent development, next up, I generated a few images and videos in Google Gemini and ChatGPT, requesting results that would look as photorealistic and "non-AI" as possible—the resulting files covered people, animals, and buildings. As before, I used copy, paste, and a few screengrabs to try and limit the metadata Pangram had access to.

Recent findings suggest that here, too, the AI identification was spot on, with all of the artificial content recognized as such, to a high level of confidence. This is perhaps not surprising: I think AI images and especially AI video still have more "tells" than AI writing, especially if you've seen a lot of it, so I wasn't expecting Pangram to fail here.

I did try experimenting with real photos that had a little bit of AI in them, what with tools like Gemini and ChatGPT now so good at image editing, as well as creating pictures from scratch. These were marked as "unsure" by Pangram, though to cut it some slack, only a small amount of the images were altered.

As with the text, the best way to beat Pangram's detection systems seems to be to include some AI embedded in human-made content. It will most likely still fail the "100% human" test, but the tests I ran showed that Pangram is less certain in these cases, or underestimates the amount of AI there actually is.

It has been revealed that increase the level of AI, and the detection gets more reliable—but if you're only using AI for a small part of whatever it is you're making, it's less worthwhile using AI tools anyway. As far as these tests go, Pangram's claims about accuracy check out, making it a useful tool if you need to ensure something is AI-free.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that “I found myself playing music that is a lot scarier,” Lawrence tells Polygon.
  • The Hunger Games is back in theaters this weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Francis Lawrence, the director of every single Hunger Games movie except the first one, likes to listen to music while working on set, with an earbud in one ear and the other left free to catch everything else that’s happening around him. While shooting the latest entry in the franchise, he added some surprising tracks to his playlist.

Sources indicate that “I found myself playing music that is a lot scarier,” Lawrence tells Polygon. That included the soundtrack from the modern horror classic, Midsommar. "Some of what I was listening to is actually some tracks from that movie.”.

The Hunger Games is back in theaters this weekend. It might be the franchise’s last entry — there are no more Suzanne Collins novels left to adapt, at least for now. Sunrise on the Reaping is a prequel centered on Katniss’ mentor, Haymitch (Joseph Zada), and it marks a return to form for the franchise, giving us the most Hunger Games arena-action since Catching Fire (long considered the franchise’s high point). It also gives the franchise an unexpected streak of horror.

Sunrise on the Reaping traces Haymitch’s failed attempts to take down the Capitol and the ensuing brutal retaliation from the government, costing him most of his friends and family. It’s the franchise’s saddest story, with a palpable sense of dread that the young adult genre rarely depicts.

Lawrence gleefully leans into these elements, while also embracing a late 1960s aesthetic that reflects the transition from the previous prequel, Ballad of the Songbirds, to the original Hunger Games movie. Again, he credits his personal playlist with leading the way.

“I started thinking of that 'White Rabbit' song from the '60s, which brought me to that era,” he says.

Sources indicate that but Lawrence's influences and ambitions go far behind the music he listened to on set. Speaking to Polygon, the director and one of the film's stars explain how Sunrise on the Reaping became one of the most ambitious and unnerving Hunger Games movies ever made.

Lawrence can't say when exactly Sunrise on the Reaping became a horror movie, simply that he leaned into it.

"I honestly can't tell you the moment when I felt this kind of pivot from the other films into that zone,” he says. "It just felt like it was coming out organically.".

Sources indicate that the film’s arena helps. Depicted as a lush and peaceful green field (whenever kids aren’t killing each other), the setting for the games lulls tributes into relaxation, hoping to hide in the trees for as long as they can. When the river’s water turns out to be poisonous, and the squirrels and birds start killing kids off, the fairy tale horror takes over.

Sources indicate that "I think part of the horror aspect came from the contrast of feeling how beautiful everything is. How beautiful it all looks, but how scary and dangerous it all really is,” says Lawrence.

Despite the gory source material, which includes a girl being crushed by an upturned chariot and multiple heads getting ripped off, Lawrence still had to tone everything down for a PG-13 audience.

It has been revealed that "In the book there's a scene of one character holding the head of a child. And I'm just thinking to myself, 'Suzanne, what are you doing to me? This is never gonna be in the movie,’” he says, laughing. “If this was my last movie, The Long Walk — that was rated R, we could do that kind of thing.”.

Lawrence ultimately decided that while they wouldn’t show gore onscreen, he could depict the gore emotionally, with the camera lingering on Haymitch’s face every time one of his friends died painfully in front of him, with him unable to do anything but watch.

"It's never really, 'It's emotionally too much.' I want to push the emotion as much as possible as long as it feels authentic and honest,” he indicates.

Sources indicate that haymitch isn’t the only character punished by the state in Sunrise on the Reaping. As a franchise, The Hunger Games is so effective because it consistently focuses on the Capitol as an authoritarian government that stifles everyone who voices a different opinion. One of these characters is Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), the victor of a previous edition of the Hunger Games who tried to take down the government’s communications system in protest. As punishment, his son is reaped (selected for a future Hunger Games tournament).

For Harrison Jr., this served as the perfect entry point to the character.

Industry observers note that "It was really locking in on Beetee as a father,” he tells Polygon. “That's a really hard thing to navigate — knowing that you were so brilliant and you were able to survive this really unfortunate system and come out alive, but yet here you are being punished for being brilliant and not being able to save your own son.".

In a recent development, harrison Jr. only has a few scenes in the movie, but he plays a key part in conveying the cruelty of the Capitol and cementing Haymitch’s position as a rebel. While he’s unable to save his son, he’s still fully committed to the rebel cause.

According to recent reports, “It's choosing and picking your battles,” he notes. “It's almost surrendering to the situation while also still being in control of what you can control.”.

Harrison Jr. took over the role from Jeffrey Wright, who played Beetee in three of the franchise’s previous films.

"I'm a huge Jeffrey Wright fan. He's one of my favorite actors of all time,” Harrison Jr. says.

The two know each other well, having worked on the movie Monster and an upcoming Jean-Michel Basquiat biopic.

"I was actually on set with him a week before I came to shoot Hunger Games, working on a different project. I talked to him about it, and he shared his excitement for Beetee. It was so funny because he was doing it while he was on his laptop, doing some coding, so I was like, 'This is so Beetee of him,’” he remarked.

With Beetee, Harrison Jr. adds another beloved franchise character to his roster. He notably voiced Scar in Mufasa: The Lion King. Surprisingly, he finds a strong connection between the mild-mannered coding genius of The Hunger Games and one of Disney’s most theatrical villains.

Industry observers note that "I kind of feel like they're one and the same. They're here to disrupt circumstances and systems that may not necessarily make sense,” he indicates.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in theaters now.

That’s part of what made Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” such a massive critical and commercial success for A24. Audiences were eager to embrace Parsons as a major newly introduced filmmaking voice — and his crew members were just as excited for the chance to work with him.

During IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “Backrooms” VFX Supervisor Edward Douglas broke down the unique workflow that he developed with Parsons during pre-production. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" broke box office records, cementing Spidey as a reliable draw at a time when most other superhero movies aren't bringing in the crowds like the used to. Now, Marvel Studios and Sony Pictures have decided to re-release the movie for the holiday season, complete with previously unseen footage that will reintroduce a cut Daredevil crossover. We just got a sneak peek at that same crossover via a picture posted to Claire Temple actor Rosario Dawson's Instagram.

Recent findings suggest that temple originally appeared in Netflix's "Daredevil" series before becoming a mainstay in that small-screen universe. The nurse not only tended to Charlie Cox's Daredevil but also his fellow Defenders: Krysten Ritter's Jessica Jones, Mike Colter's Luke Cage, and Finn Jones' Iron Fist. (Temple didn't appear in Jon Bernthal's "The Punisher" series.) Alas, the Netflix series were all canceled by early 2019. Since then, Cox's Matt Murdock has returned in the Disney+ show "Daredevil: Born Again," in addition to making a brief cameo in 2021's "Spider-Man: No Way Home.".

In a recent development, originally, "Brand Fresh Day" also featured a crossover with the erstwhile Netflix "Daredevil" series. Sadly, a scene that featured Temple was removed from the final cut prior to its debut in July 2026. Now, however, that scene has been reinstated for the extended cut, awkwardly titled "Spider-Man: [Brand New] Brand New Day," which hits theaters on December 4, 2026.

It has been revealed that per The Hollywood Reporter, "Spider-Man: [Brand Latest] Brand New Day" features 10 minutes of extra footage, most of which remains a mystery. One thing we do know, however, is that Rosario Dawson's Claire Temple cameo has been reinstated.

The actor took to Instagram to post a photo from the scene in question, which shows Temple standing alongside Tom Holland's Spider-Man inside a hospital room. This clearly takes place at the end of the movie, following Spidey's tumultuous final showdown with Sadie Sink's Jean Grey. Beyond that, however, Dawson didn't reveal much about what happens in the footage. "So excited to enjoy this record-breaking movie on the significant screen," she wrote in her caption."[...] with an extended cut of fresh scenes and surprises... Ahhhh!".

Industry observers note that dawson previously revealed how she felt about being cut from "Brand Latest Day," saying that she had a BTS post ready to go about her time on-set that she ultimately had to scrap. Clearly, the actor was disappointed, which isn't surprising considering "Brand New Day" absolutely ruled the box office. Still, as she stated at the time (via Variety) "Because everybody's in it, it still means that my character is somewhere in that same universe, and I really love that. So, I hope I get to be Claire again." Now, with her footage being added back into the movie for the re-release, she has even more reason to be hopeful.

With Rosario Dawson's Claire Temple appearing in the "Spider-Man: Brand Upcoming Day" re-release, the question becomes whether she'll show up again as the Marvel Cinematic Universe enters its next phase. As of now, "Daredevil: Born Again" has been canceled at Disney+, which means the upcoming third season will be its last. Thus far, Claire Temple hasn't appeared in the revival series, but there have been a few oblique references to a friendly nurse. Whether she'll show up in "Born Again" Season 3 remains unclear, but it wouldn't be surprising if she did.

Sources indicate that with the show having been axed, however, Temple's MCU future remains even more uncertain. Perhaps if we get a fifth Tom Holland Spidey outing, she might come back. But such a film is also yet to be confirmed. "Brand New Day" producer Amy Pascal has one rule for making another movie, which essentially amounts to focusing on one film at a time. Still, with "Brand New Day" becoming nothing short of a phenomenon, it seems almost certain Sony Pictures and Marvel Studios will want to get Holland back for another outing ASAP.

Sources indicate that indeed, "Brand Fresh Day" has made $2.5 billion at the global box office, and the re-release will likely bring in a decent bit of extra profit. Hence, with "Born Again" ending after its next season, a "Brand New Day" sequel seems like the most likely venue for a Temple return. For now, though, we'll have to await further news.

Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1358 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change.
  • In a recent development, download your playlist as a .txt file.
  • Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

In a recent development, download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

In a recent development, download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

In a recent development, sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of new-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection.".

Recent findings suggest that on Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Users can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

If you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Pick your speaker on your wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Recent findings suggest that plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:.

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

Force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

Set your levels with the mixer’s faders.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:.

Mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

My cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

It's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:.

Your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:.

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

In a recent development, you have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

In a recent development, this isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

How to hide the newly introduced macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (329 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override.
  • In a recent development, if you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar.
  • I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

In a recent development, if you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:.

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false.

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

The command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:.

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR.

Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future update.

Recent findings suggest that not a fan of this on macOS 27.3 beta 2. #4672. Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1158 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Indiewire ↗ Open Full Page

Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Film is always a collaborative medium, but one of the special things about animation is that you can craft incredibly nuanced performances with people who never get to meet.
  • “Wildwood” director Travis Knight did a lot of the directing of his voice cast in lockdown Zooms, and hodge-podge recording setups, where it can be hard to remember that you’re developing something that needs to spiritually connect to the animation, whether existing animatics already exist or not.
  • Industry observers note that “It asks something very different of an actor, which is challenging because an actor can bring so much to performance before they even utter a word,” Knight told IndieWire on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Film is always a collaborative medium, but one of the special things about animation is that you can craft incredibly nuanced performances with people who never get to meet. Voice acting in animation is a discipline in its own right — as legends like Mel Blanc and Eric Bauza show — where actors impart a kind of electric energy that carries through into the art style of what they’re voicing. So is voice directing. And the secret to both is in providing foundations for animators to build something bigger.

“Wildwood” director Travis Knight did a lot of the directing of his voice cast in lockdown Zooms, and hodge-podge recording setups, where it can be hard to remember that you’re developing something that needs to spiritually connect to the animation, whether existing animatics already exist or not. There isn’t the same kind of immersiveness for actors that live-action sets, costumes, and the basic pleasure of getting to read lines against other actors all provide. They have to build it from scratch. Related Stories Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons Aaron Pierre on ‘Lanterns,’ the DC Shake-Up, and Landing a Role in Ryan Gosling’s ‘Star Wars’ Movie.

Industry observers note that “It asks something very different of an actor, which is challenging because an actor can bring so much to performance before they even utter a word,” Knight told IndieWire on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “So when you cast these things, it’s really interesting because sometimes the things we love about actors are not their voice; it’s everything else. So we will always listen, we’ll take clips from actors’ other films and their interviews, and we’ll put them against a design of a character.”.

According to recent reports, hearing a voice against a design can be revelatory, Knight believes, because it can teach a director and an animation team about who a character really is, whether a performer is really going to work or not, even before they step into the booth. It’s also an crucial way to help sort the whole of an ensemble so that actors occupy different aural frequencies and accents, and don’t sound too similar. You want to really be able to feel the difference between Carey Mulligan’s powerfully sinister Alexandra and Angela Bassett’s regal General.

And then, once the voice cast is in the booth, it’s also on the director and the team to help each voice actor sketch out all the different permutations of emotion the animators will then use as inspiration, and as tools.

“You’ll get the scene 30, 40, 50 different ways,” Knight said. “It takes forever. But, in the end, if you can do it properly, it feels like these characters are living in the same scene at the same time. And then it comes down to the animator to try to figure out how they can match the beauty of the vocal performance with the physical performance.”.

That’s the normal process for feature animation: finding compelling voices, matching them with a design that feels spiritually connected to that voice, covering the performance many different ways, and then assembling a template for animators to build off of. And it’s the director, really, who has to hold in their head the many ways that the disparate parts will all come together.

It has been revealed that “An animator is an actor, but they’re just acting through their hands and through a puppet, and it’s two actors collaborating to create a complete performance. But oftentimes it happens across space, across time. And when it comes together in a harmonious way, it’s really beautiful because this thing seems like it’s completely alive,” Knight mentioned.

But sometimes, voice actors’ performances do get to be alive together. That was a key creative choice that director Leah Nelson made for “Tangles” — it’s hard to argue with the logic of putting Abbi Jacobson, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, and Bryan Cranston all in a room together to act out an earnest family drama, even if there’s a bit of mic bleed.

“I’m so glad we [put them together]. And it wasn’t that hard. It took a little bit of scheduling Tetris to get it done, but it was so worthwhile,” Nelson told IndieWire. “Abbi does a ton of voice work, and often they’re alone and not even able to have someone to read against them. Sometimes they’re just doing the lines and sort of jumping around. And what I ultimately wanted was to have this really naturalistic dialogue.”.

Industry observers note that “Tangles” boasts naturalism when it comes to sound, from bespoke foley to overlapping banter that isn’t meant to be precisely understood but to convey the chaos of one’s own (infuriating, loving) family. So Nelson and her team embraced the ways actors can build on each other, and even on improv, in recording the dialogue.

Industry observers note that “A lot of humor came out of giving them time to not only play with the dialogue but to play with each other. But also, those really intimate and difficult moments of the film, they could look in each other’s eyes and work through those moments. That was important to me, and it was important to them as well. So it was an experience we all went through together.”.

The one downside of treating recording sessions more like the rehearsals for a play is the risk of wrecking takes. “We spent a lot of time at the table trying to hold [our reactions] in or like, ‘Don’t sneeze! Nobody move!’” Nelson joked. “But I didn’t want it to sound like there was so much suturing; the mastery of the dialogue editing to make it all sound naturalistic, so we also did a lot of work to make that happen. But what we had to work with felt very naturalistic to begin with.”.

The ultimate example of naturalistic voice acting, however, might be on display in “Wildwood.” Knight’s own son was a newborn while the team was laying down track for the film, which made him the perfect actor for the role of kidnapped Baby Mac.

“I essentially chased him around the house with a digital recorder. Sometimes with my iPhone. I was just trying to coax things out of him, make him laugh and giggle and verbalize. And the thing about babies is that they’re constantly trying to make sense of the world,” Knight said. “They’re always babbling and trying to make shapes with their mouths. So we have a lot of that babbling in the movie, and it helped make it feel naturalistic.”.

It speaks to the wide-ranging power of voice acting in animation: you can get to naturalism through a grounded collaboration between actors, an actor in complete isolation, or hitting “record” on an iPhone while you’re changing a diaper.

“Wildwood” is now in theaters. “Tangles” releases in theaters on January 15, 2027.

Don't go to the old reaping site with your buddies and reminisce if you haven't seen "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Spoilers ahead!

We've known, for quite some time now, that Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss Everdeen and Josh Hutcherson's Peeta Mellark would return in the highly anticipated big-screen prequel "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." If you've read the book, you know that they come back for an epilogue, and in late October 2026 — just about a month before the film's release — Lawrence opened up about the experience and confirmed that Woody Harrelson, who plays the older version of "Sunrise's" protagonist Haymitch Abernathy in the original Hunger Games films, is also part of the scene. So ... what happens?

There are some differences between the epilogue in the book and the film adaptation helmed by Francis Lawrence, but the gist is the same — and I'll return to those differences later on. After we see how Haymitch wins his games and how the Capitol punishes him for attempting to destroy the 50th Games arena — Haymitch attempts to blow up a water tank and essentially drown the machine, but safeguards stop his blueprint from going through, and his family and loved ones are killed upon his return to District 12 — we see Harrelson's Haymitch approach an ivy-covered structure that's the old site of the annual reaping that chose one boy and one girl to compete in the deadly Games. He's joined by Katniss and Peeta, who wish him a happy birthday; it's a major plot point in "Sunrise" that reaping day always falls on Haymitch's birthdays. They thank him for everything, and Haymitch says "Nevermore" before departing.

Putting the prequel "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" aside — because none of the characters I'm talking about were alive during that story — it makes complete sense for Katniss and Peeta to show up to close out Haymitch's standalone movie. The three are, for all intents and purposes during the original Hunger Games timeline, a package deal. We see, at the end of "Sunrise on the Reaping," that Haymitch arrives home in District 12 and sees the coffins of his fellow tributes, and we also see a montage of Joseph Zada's younger take on the character overseeing the delivery of coffins that are clearly tributes he was forced to mentor as a former victor.

Sources indicate that by the time we get to the 74th Games, Haymitch is constantly drunk and imbibes to survive, telling his tributes his only advice is that they stay alive. When he and Katniss click, though, he starts to wonder if these tributes have what it takes ... and thanks to a plot conceived by him and Peeta that presents Katniss and Peeta as star-crossed lovers forced to compete, they get to jointly win the Games.

That next year, only previous victors can be reaped, and Katniss and Peeta go back in to fight, though Haymitch hatches a strategy with other rebels to break them out of the arena. Though Peeta is kidnapped, tortured, and brainwashed by the Capitol, they eventually rescue him and take down the Capitol, ultimately returning to District 12 to live out the rest of their days together.

Industry observers note that in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," this ending for Haymitch, Katniss, and Peeta feels hopeful and optimistic. Suzanne Collins, the author of the franchise, takes a darker approach in the literary epilogues for both "Mockingjay" and "Sunrise on the Reaping." In "Mockingjay," Katniss notes that both she and Peeta have post-traumatic stress disorder and still suffer greatly, experiencing night terrors and other symptoms. In the book version of "Sunrise," Haymitch speaks directly to the reader about how he didn't even want to care about his two tributes initially because he felt too broken, but he was worn down. "I didn't want to let them in, her and Peeta, but the walls of a person's heart are not impregnable, not if they have ever known love," he muses before mourning his one true love, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak in the film), who was poisoned by Capitol forces when Haymitch initially returned to District 12 as a victor.

Beyond that, Haymitch is blunt about the way that chronic drinking has affected his body. "I'm not sure I'll be here in the old therebefore much longer. My liver's wrecked and I only dry out when the train's late," he claims. "I drink differently these days, though, less to forget, more out of habit. When my time comes, it comes, but I've no idea when that will be." Still, Haymitch gets a relatively happy ending with Katniss and Peeta.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters.

Latest Update: The 10 Best Action War Movies of All Time, Ranked

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there’s a risk with making a war movie also feel like an action one, especially if a filmmaker wants to have things feel anti-war, and sure, most war movies should be at least a little anti-war, otherwise they might run the risk of feeling like propaganda.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there’s a risk with making a war movie also feel like an action one, especially if a filmmaker wants to have things feel anti-war, and sure, most war movies should be at least a little anti-war, otherwise they might run the risk of feeling like propaganda. If it’s a fictional war, or if it’s something that really rewrites history, and it’s all done well, then maybe it’s okay to have some fun with the war genre, though.

Recent findings suggest that the following movies do it well, and differ from the likes of Platoon, Saving Private Ryan, and Das Boot, all of which have moments of combat and tension, but are a little harder to label as “action movies” in the traditional sense. These are the best action war movies of all time, and an “action war movie” is just what you'd expect: something that belongs to both of those genres (and maybe one or two others at the same time, too).

It has been revealed that even though John Woo is one of the all-time greatest action movie directors, he’s also so prolific that certain movies in his filmography tend to get a bit overlooked, especially those without gunfights, which is the style of action he’s best known for. If only this were an opportunity to rave about Last Hurrah for Chivalry, but alas, that’s “just” a martial arts movie, and it doesn’t really have anything that makes it qualify as a war film as well.

But hey, at least there’s Red Cliff, which does have tons of hand-to-hand fighting, thanks to its historical setting, but it’s all on a much bigger scale than Last Hurrah for Chivalry. You do have to watch both parts of Red Cliff to fully appreciate it, naturally, though if you want one singled out, may as well make it the first part, released in 2008 (the second part from 2009, Kill Bill-style, is a little slower-paced and maybe not quite as impressive with its action).

Sources indicate that calling Black Hawk Down realistic as far as its historical accuracy is concerned might be questionable, but calling it realistic in terms of how it captures relatively modern-day combat isn't out of the question. Or maybe grounded and visceral are slightly better words to use to describe how Black Hawk Down feels, because the film depicts the Battle of Mogadishu, and pretty much refuses to let up pacing-wise once stated battle begins.

That does mean Black Hawk Down is exhausting, but with a purpose. It dramatizes (and takes some liberties with) an actual event, and feels grittier with its presentation than so many other war films made around the same time, or before, or since… or, well, any time, really. And for what it’s worth, there’s a pretty impressive ensemble cast here, especially with some who became more famous in the years following 2001.

High-concept premises don’t get much higher than the one found in G.I. Samurai, and the commitment to that premise is admirable. It’s a time travel movie that involves soldiers from the 20th century going back to samurai times. While there, they inevitably have to fight in a very different sort of combat, concerning samurai battles (it’s in the title and stuff) of the sort fought in the 15th and 16th centuries in Japan.

Speaking of things being in the title, it’s nice when a movie doesn’t lie to you, and you know what you're in for with just a couple of words. There are G.I. soldiers and there are samurai, and they fight. That is G.I. Samurai. It’s a good time, featuring plenty of action and technically being a mash-up of two different sorts of war movies at the same time, thanks to the time travel angle.

It’d be easiest to describe Wings as a World War I melodrama with quite a bit of romance as well, thanks to it having a love triangle at its center, but there is still action here. For something that’s now very close to a century old, it’s quite remarkable to behold, with the dogfighting sequences being some of the best parts of the movie, and the parts that hold up the best all this time later.

For something that’s now very close to a century old, it’s quite remarkable to behold, with the dogfighting sequences being some of the best parts of the movie.

Sources indicate that also, Wings was the first movie to win Best Picture at the first Academy Awards ceremony, though it didn’t set a precedent for such movies (like, those partly belonging to the action genre) to win that award often. And it won alongside another 1927 release, Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans, with Wings getting "Outstanding Picture" and the latter getting the unique and soon-to-be-retired award of "Unique and Artistic Picture." Both are romances, but very different kinds of romance films. Anyway, if you're into older movies, Wings, though not perfect, is still a must-watch.

Recent findings suggest that since it’s set the year after the Vietnam War ended, Eastern Condors kind of gets around being a Vietnam War movie of sorts that proves bombastic and entertaining, in contrast to most Vietnam War movies, which play up the horror, misery, and moral complexities of the conflict. The premise involves prisoners getting the option of being excused, a little like another action/war movie from 1967, and that’ll be mentioned shortly.

But a good premise is a good premise, so that’s okay. Here, the characters go into Vietnam and undertake a dangerous mission to destroy missiles that U.S. forces abandoned there. When there, lots of shootouts and then even some hand-to-hand fight scenes ensue. Eastern Condors is maximalist, and then it’s also remarkably generous with just how much action it features throughout (almost exhausting, but in a good way).

Four years on from Black Hawk Down, Ridley Scott made another war movie with Kingdom of Heaven, but it’s worth mentioning both, since the two do have quite a bit by way of action and spectacle. As for differences, though, this one goes back much further in time, since Kingdom of Heaven takes place during the Crusades, with the plot following a blacksmith who gets swept up in the complicated and alarmingly large-scale war.

Sources indicate that there’s intrigue here and political drama alongside all the battle sequences, and if you watch the director’s cut (much better than the theatrical cut), the non-action stuff is quite compelling, too. But if you're after action and battles, that side of Kingdom of Heaven does shine bright, since Ridley Scott, though not the most consistent of filmmakers, can generally helm this kind of movie better than the vast majority of well-known directors out there.

John Woo is back here, on this ranking, with Bullet in the Head being a bit more of a classic kind of John Woo film compared to Red Cliff. Like, it’s got shootouts, basically. But then it differs a little from some of his other heroic bloodshed movies because it gets arguably even darker than the likes of A Better Tomorrow and The Killer (Hard Boiled is just a blast, though… violent, sure, but mostly fun).

Bullet in the Head is more despairing because the lead characters end up fleeing Hong Kong, and find that it makes their experiences worse, since they end up entangled in the Vietnam War. It begins as a crime film, and becomes a Vietnam War film. And then all the while, whichever genre it’s focusing on, it retains a pretty high level of action throughout. If you don’t mind watching something a bit depressing, it’s very much worthwhile.

Industry observers note that while all the other action movies Michael Mann’s directed can be called crime/thriller films as well as action-related, The Last of the Mohicans very much isn’t a crime film, and it stands out among the other Michael Mann action films for taking place so long ago. It’s set during the 18th century, and the conflict everything plays out against is the French and Indian War, which involved the British Empire, the French Empire, and certain Native American tribes.

Industry observers note that it’s a real blend of genres for something that clocks in at under two hours, given it also works as something of a war and adventure film, and romance is pretty central to the narrative, too. The Last of the Mohicans could've stood to be a little longer, because it’s like an epic movie just without the epic runtime, but at least what is here is remarkable, and honestly pretty difficult to fault.

The Dirty Dozen was alluded to earlier, back when talking about Eastern Condors, since they share that whole basic premise of “Hey, you shady guys doing this really dangerous thing that might kill you all, but if you survive, your crimes will be pardoned.” It has a remarkable cast and is very well-structured as an action/adventure/war movie, with the mission taking place in the final act, and noted mission involving going behind enemy lines during World War II.

It has been revealed that before that final act, things are still exciting and interesting, but there is a lot of set-up and character development (developing some very eccentric characters at that, too). The Dirty Dozen is quite fun for something ultimately rather dark and intense, with an odd sort of tone struck here, yet the movie thankfully makes it work. And it all packs a fairly solid punch even close to six decades on from its release.

It has been revealed that yeah, so it’s not historically accurate, of course, but Braveheart does have a ton of action, and it also builds into something of a war movie as it goes along (like Wings, it was a Best Picture winner, too). It begins as a movie about revenge, but that quest for revenge ultimately balloons into something much grander, and that’s when all the war and battle scenes really come into it.

William Wallace (a real person, but again, this film’s not exactly a biopic) is the central character here, and he ends up inspiring a rebellion – and leading an army – in the wake of getting violent revenge against some English soldiers responsible for the death of the woman he loved. Those are the basics. And Braveheart isn't quite basic, but it almost is. It’s straightforward, yet works incredibly well for what it is, and the spectacle here is something to behold.

I recently switched music streamers from Apple Music to Tidal. I like Tidal's strict anti-AI features, the fact that it pays higher royalties to artists than other major streamers, and its focus on high quality audio. I wrote a post featuring eight hacks for Tidal users, but I wanted to highlight one in particular: How to transfer playlists without paying anything.

It has been revealed that download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Sources indicate that download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Sources indicate that run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sources indicate that sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

It has been revealed that have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

The only iCloud+ tier that doesn’t include higher limits is the $0.99/month strategy.

iCloud+ already provided far more than just increased cloud storage, but with iOS 27.3 it’s set to be an asset for AI power customers too.
